Judges 17:12 Micah made the Levite special, and the young man became his priest, living in Micah's house.
Judges 17:13 Then Micah said, "Now I know that God will be good to me because I have a Levite as my priest."

Judges 18:1 During that time, Israel had no king. The Danites were looking for land to live on because they had not yet received a share of land among Israel's tribes.
Judges 18:2 The Danites sent five brave family men from Zorah and Eshtaol to explore the land. They told them, "Go and look over the land." When they reached Mount Ephraim and Micah's house, they stayed there.
Judges 18:3 While they were near Micah's house, they recognized the Levite's voice, so they went there and asked him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? And what do you have here?"
Judges 18:4 He told them, "Micah has treated me this way; he has hired me, and I am his priest."
Judges 18:5 They asked him, "Please ask God to guide us so we know if our journey will be successful."
Judges 18:6 The priest told them, "Go peacefully: God knows the path you take."
Judges 18:7 The five men left and went to Laish, where they saw the people living safely, like the Zidonians, without worry and secure; there was no leader to make them feel guilty about anything; they were distant from the Zidonians and did not interact with anyone.
Judges 18:8 They went to their brothers in Zorah and Eshtaol, and their brothers asked them, "What do you say?"
Judges 18:9 They said, "Get up, so we can attack them. We've seen the land, and it's really good. Why wait? Don't be lazy to go take over the land."
Judges 18:10 When you go, you will find a safe people and a big land. God has given it to you; a place where you lack nothing that is on the earth.
Judges 18:11 From there, six hundred men from the Danite family, from Zorah and Eshtaol, equipped for battle, left.
Judges 18:12 They went and camped at Kirjathjearim in Judah. That's why they named the place Mahanehdan, and it's still called that today. It's near Kirjathjearim.
Judges 18:13 They traveled from there to Mount Ephraim and arrived at Micah's house.
Judges 18:14 The five men who explored Laish replied to their brothers, "Do you realize that in these homes there is a priest's robe, household gods, a carved idol, and a metal idol? Think about what you should do now."
Judges 18:15 They went there, came to the young Levite's house, to Micah's house, and greeted him.
Judges 18:16 The six hundred armed men from the tribe of Dan stood at the gate entrance.
Judges 18:17 The five men who went to explore the land climbed up, went there, and took the carved idol, the priestly garment, the household gods, and the cast idol, while the priest waited at the entrance of the gate with the six hundred armed men.
Judges 18:18 These people went into Micah's house, took the carved idol, the priestly garment, the household gods, and the metal idol. Then the priest asked them, "What are you doing?"
Judges 18:19 They told him, "Be quiet, put your hand over your mouth, and come with us. Be our leader and priest. Isn't it better to be a priest for one man's house or a whole tribe and family in Israel?"
Judges 18:20 The priest was happy, and he took the special vest, the household gods, and the carved idol, and joined the people.
Judges 18:21 They turned and left, putting the children, the animals, and the carts ahead of them.
Judges 18:22 When they were far from Micah's house, the men living near Micah gathered and caught up with the people of Dan.
Judges 18:23 They called out to the people of Dan. They turned around and asked Micah, "What's wrong with you that you come with such a group?"
Judges 18:24 He said, "You've taken my gods that I made and the priest, and left. What else do I have left? Why do you ask, 'What's wrong with you?'"
Judges 18:25 The people of Dan told him, "Don't let us hear your voice, or some angry men might attack you, and you and your family could die."
Judges 18:26 The Danites continued traveling. When Micah realized they were too strong for him, he turned around and went back home.
Judges 18:27 They took what Micah had made and his priest, and went to Laish, a peaceful and safe town. They attacked them with swords and set the city on fire.
Judges 18:28 No one could save them because they were far from Zidon, not involved with anyone, and in a valley near Bethrehob. They built a city there and lived in it.
Judges 18:29 They named the city Dan after their ancestor Dan, born to Israel, but the city was first called Laish.
Judges 18:30 The Dan tribe set up an idol, and Jonathan, Gershom's son and Manasseh's grandson, served as priest with his sons for the Dan tribe until the land was captured.
Judges 18:31 They put up Micah's carved idol, which he had made, for as long as God's house was in Shiloh.

Judges 19:1 During that time, when Israel had no king, a Levite staying near Mount Ephraim took a woman from Bethlehem in Judah to be his concubine.
Judges 19:2 His partner was unfaithful to him, left him, and went to her father's house in Bethlehem of Judah, staying there four months.
Judges 19:3 Her husband got up, followed her to talk kindly and to take her back, with his helper and two donkeys. She took him to her father's house, and the girl's father was happy to see him.
Judges 19:4 The girl's father, who was also his father-in-law, kept him with him, and he stayed there for three days. They ate, drank, and slept there.
Judges 19:5 On the fourth day, when they got up early, he got ready to leave. The girl's father said to his son-in-law, "Have some bread to feel better, and then you can go."
Judges 19:6 They sat and ate and drank together because the girl's father told the man, "Please be happy, stay overnight, and enjoy yourself."
Judges 19:7 When the man got up to leave, his father-in-law convinced him, so he stayed there another night.
Judges 19:8 He got up early on the fifth day to leave, but the girl's father said, "Please, relax and eat." So they stayed until the afternoon and both had something to eat.
Judges 19:9 When the man got ready to leave with his concubine and servant, his father-in-law, the girl's father, told him, "Look, it is almost evening. Please stay the night. The day is almost over. Stay here and be happy. Tomorrow you can leave early to go home."
Judges 19:10 The man didn't stay the night; instead, he got up, left, and went near Jebus, now called Jerusalem. He had two saddled donkeys with him, and his partner was also with him.
Judges 19:11 When they were near Jebus, it was getting late; the servant told his master, "Please, let's go into this Jebusite city and spend the night there."
Judges 19:12 His boss told him, "We won't go into a foreign city not belonging to the Israelites; we'll keep going to Gibeah."
Judges 19:13 He said to his servant, "Come, let's go stay the night in one of these towns, either Gibeah or Ramah."
Judges 19:14 They moved on and continued their journey. The sun set on them near Gibeah, a town in Benjamin's territory.
Judges 19:15 They went there to stay in Gibeah. When he entered, he sat down in the city street because no one took them into his home for the night.
Judges 19:16 Look, an old man coming from his work in the field at evening was from Mount Ephraim; he was staying in Gibeah, although the local men were from Benjamin's tribe.
Judges 19:17 When he looked up, he saw a traveler in the city street; and the old man asked, "Where are you going? And where did you come from?"
Judges 19:18 He said to him, "We are traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to the area of Mount Ephraim. That is where I am from. I have been to Bethlehem in Judah and now I am on my way to God's house, but no one has offered to take me in."
Judges 19:19 We have both straw and food for our donkeys; there is also bread and wine for me, for your servant woman, and for the young man with your workers: we lack nothing.
Judges 19:20 The old man said, "May you have peace. I will take care of all your needs. Just don't sleep outside."
Judges 19:21 He took him into his house, fed the donkeys, they washed their feet, and they ate and drank.
Judges 19:22 While they were enjoying themselves, suddenly the city men, some wicked fellows, surrounded the house. They pounded on the door and said to the homeowner, the old man, "Send out the man who came to your house, so we can meet him."
Judges 19:23 The man who owned the house went outside to them and said, "No, my friends, please don't do such an evil thing. Since this man is a guest in my home, please don't act so foolishly."
Judges 19:24 Look, here is my daughter who is a virgin, and his partner; I will send them out to you, and you can use them as you please, but do not do such a disgraceful thing to this man.
Judges 19:25 The men did not listen to him, so the man took his woman and gave her to them. They mistreated her all night until morning, and when dawn came, they released her.
Judges 19:26 The woman arrived at daybreak and collapsed at the door of the house where her man stayed, until morning came.
Judges 19:27 In the morning, her husband got up, opened the doors of the house, and left to go on his way. He saw that his concubine woman was lying at the house door with her hands on the doorstep.
Judges 19:28 He said to her, "Get up, let's go." But she did not answer. So he lifted her onto a donkey, got up, and went home.
Judges 19:29 When he entered his home, he took a knife, grabbed his concubine, cut her and her bones into twelve parts, and sent them throughout Israel.
Judges 19:30 Everyone who saw it agreed that nothing like this has happened or been seen since the Israelites left Egypt. Think about it, talk it over, and decide what to do.

Judges 20:1 All the Israelites came together as one group, from Dan to Beersheba including the people of Gilead, to meet with God in Mizpah.
Judges 20:2 The leaders of the people from all the tribes of Israel came together in the meeting, a total of 400,000 soldiers ready for battle.
Judges 20:3 The people of Benjamin learned that the people of Israel had gone to Mizpeh. Then the people of Israel asked, "Tell us, how did this evil happen?"
Judges 20:4 The Levite, the woman's husband who was killed, replied, "I went to Gibeah in Benjamin with my concubine to stay overnight."
Judges 20:5 The men of Gibeah attacked me, surrounded the house at night thinking to kill me, and they raped my concubine so that she died.
Judges 20:6 I took my wife who was not my first wife, cut her into parts, and sent her pieces all over Israel's land because they did shameful and foolish things in Israel.
Judges 20:7 Look, you are all Israel's children; share your advice and thoughts here.
Judges 20:8 All the people stood up together and said, "None of us will go to our tents or go back to our homes."
Judges 20:9 But now, here's our plan for Gibeah: we will decide by drawing lots who will attack it.
Judges 20:10 We will pick ten men from every hundred in all of Israel's tribes, a hundred from every thousand, and a thousand from every ten thousand, to get food for the people, so they can act when they arrive at Gibeah in Benjamin because of the foolish things done in Israel.
Judges 20:11 All the men of Israel came together against the city, united as if they were one person.
Judges 20:12 The tribes of Israel sent people throughout the tribe of Benjamin asking, "What is this evil thing that has happened among you?"
Judges 20:13 Now give us the evil men of Gibeah so we can kill them and remove evil from Israel. But the tribe of Benjamin wouldn't listen to their fellow Israelites.
Judges 20:14 The people of Benjamin came from the cities to Gibeah to fight the people of Israel.
Judges 20:15 At that time, 26,000 soldiers from Benjamin's cities were counted, not including 700 select men from Gibeah.
Judges 20:16 In this group there were seven hundred skilled left-handed men; each could sling a stone at a hair and not miss.
Judges 20:17 The men of Israel, not including Benjamin, totaled 400,000 swordsmen, all ready for battle.
Judges 20:18 The Israelites got up, went to God's house, asked God for advice, and said, "Who among us should go first to fight the people of Benjamin?" And God answered, "Judah should go first."
Judges 20:19 The Israelites got up in the morning and set up camp near Gibeah.
Judges 20:20 The Israelite men went to fight against Benjamin and lined up in battle formation at Gibeah.
Judges 20:21 The Benjamin people came out of Gibeah and killed twenty-two thousand Israelite men that day.
Judges 20:22 The Israelite soldiers cheered themselves up and lined up for battle again in the same place as they did the first time.
Judges 20:23 The Israelites cried before God until evening, then asked God for advice, saying, "Should I fight against my brother Benjamin again?" And God said, "Fight against them."
Judges 20:24 On the second day, the Israelites approached the Benjaminites.
Judges 20:25 Benjamin attacked them from Gibeah for the second time and killed eighteen thousand Israelite men who had swords.
Judges 20:26 All the Israelites and the people went to God's house, cried, sat before God, and fasted all day until evening. They also gave burnt and peace offerings to God.
Judges 20:27 The children of Israel asked God, because the ark of God's covenant was there at that time.
Judges 20:28 Phinehas, who was Eleazar's son and Aaron's grandson, asked at that time, "Should I go fight the Benjamites, my relatives, again, or stop?" And God said, "Go, for tomorrow I will give them to you."
Judges 20:29 Israel placed ambushers all around Gibeah.
Judges 20:30 On the third day, the Israelites advanced against the Benjamites and prepared for battle near Gibeah, just like before.
Judges 20:31 The Benjamin kids came out to fight the people, got lured away from the city, and started to attack and kill the people on the roads, like they did before. One road led to God's house and another to Gibeah in the open fields, and they killed about thirty Israelite men.
Judges 20:32 The people of Benjamin said, "They are beaten like before." But the people of Israel said, "Let's run away and lure them from the city to the roads."
Judges 20:33 All the men of Israel got up, got ready for battle at Baaltamar, and Israel's ambushers came out of their hiding spots, from the fields of Gibeah.
Judges 20:34 Ten thousand picked men from Israel attacked Gibeah, and the fight was fierce, but they didn't realize that danger was close.
Judges 20:35 God struck down Benjamin in front of Israel, and on that day, the Israelites killed 25,100 Benjamite men who fought with swords.
Judges 20:36 The children of Benjamin realized they were beaten because the Israelite men stepped aside for them, trusting the ambushers they had placed near Gibeah.
Judges 20:37 The ambushers hurried and attacked Gibeah; the ambushers moved in and struck down the whole city with their swords.
Judges 20:38 The men of Israel and those hiding had a signal: when they saw a big smoke fire from the city, they would attack.
Judges 20:39 When the Israelite men pulled back in the fight, the Benjaminites started to strike and kill about thirty Israelite men, because they thought, "Surely we're beating them as before."
Judges 20:40 But when fire started to rise from the city with a column of smoke, the people of Benjamin looked back and saw the city's fire going up to the sky.
Judges 20:41 When the Israelite men turned back, the Benjamites were shocked because they realized disaster had struck them.
Judges 20:42 So they ran away from the Israelites toward the desert path, but the battle caught up with them; and they destroyed those who came from the cities right among them.
Judges 20:43 So they surrounded the Benjamites, chased them, and easily crushed them near Gibeah as the sun was rising.
Judges 20:44 Eighteen thousand men from Benjamin died; they were all brave soldiers.
Judges 20:45 They turned and ran to the desert, to Rimmon's rock. They killed five thousand men on the roads and chased them to Gidom, killing two thousand more.
Judges 20:46 On that day, 25,000 fighting men from Benjamin died; all were brave warriors.
Judges 20:47 Six hundred men turned and ran to the wilderness to the rock Rimmon, and stayed at the rock Rimmon for four months.
Judges 20:48 The Israelite men attacked the Benjamites again, killing them with swords, including the men of every city, animals, and everything else they found. They also burned down all the cities they went to.

Judges 21:1 The men of Israel promised in Mizpeh, "None of us will let our daughters marry men from Benjamin."
Judges 21:2 The people went to God's house, stayed there until evening, raised their voices, and cried a lot.
Judges 21:3 And said, O God of Israel, why has this happened in Israel, that today one tribe is missing in Israel?
Judges 21:4 The next day, the people got up early, built an altar there, and made burnt offerings and peace offerings.
Judges 21:5 The Israelites asked, "Who from all Israel's tribes didn't join the group to meet with God? They had strongly promised to kill anyone who didn't come to Mizpeh to meet with God."
Judges 21:6 The people of Israel felt sorry for their brother Benjamin and said, "Today one tribe is missing from Israel."
Judges 21:7 What can we do to find wives for those who are left, since we have promised with a strong oath that we will not let them marry our daughters?
Judges 21:8 They asked, "Who from the tribes of Israel didn't come to Mizpeh to God?" And no one from Jabeshgilead came to the camp for the meeting.
Judges 21:9 The people were counted, and look, no one from Jabesh-gilead was there.
Judges 21:10 The group sent twelve thousand brave men and told them, "Go and defeat the people of Jabeshgilead with the sword, including the women and children."
Judges 21:11 This is what you must do: You must kill every man and every woman who has slept with a man.
Judges 21:12 They found 400 young women in Jabesh Gilead who had never slept with a man, and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh in Canaan.
Judges 21:13 The whole group sent messengers to talk to the Benjamite people at the rock Rimmon, inviting them peacefully.
Judges 21:14 Benjamin returned then, and they were given wives from the saved women of Jabeshgilead, but there were not enough women for them.
Judges 21:15 The people felt sorry for Benjamin because God had caused a split among the tribes of Israel.
Judges 21:16 Then the community leaders asked, "What will we do to find wives for the remaining men when the women of Benjamin have been killed?"
Judges 21:17 They said, "There must be a share for the survivors of Benjamin, so that a tribe is not wiped out from Israel."
Judges 21:18 But we can't give them our daughters as wives because the Israelites have made a promise, saying, "May the man who gives a wife to Benjamin be cursed."
Judges 21:19 They said, "Look, every year there's a festival for God in Shiloh, north of Bethel, east of the road leading from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah."
Judges 21:20 They told the people of Benjamin, "Go and hide in the vineyards."
Judges 21:21 Look, and if the girls from Shiloh come out to dance, then come out of the vineyards, and each of you catch a wife from the girls of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.
Judges 21:22 When their fathers or brothers come to complain to us, we will ask them to forgive them for our sake: we didn't save a wife for each man in the war because you didn't give them their wives now, so you aren't to blame.
Judges 21:23 The men of Benjamin did this, and each took a wife from the dancing women they captured. They went back to their land, fixed their cities, and lived there.
Judges 21:24 The Israelites left from there at that time, each person to their own tribe and family, and each went to their own land.
Judges 21:25 At that time, there was no king in Israel; everyone just did what they thought was right.

Ruth 1:1 During the time when judges led, a famine struck the land. A man from Bethlehem in Judah moved to live in Moab with his wife and two sons.
Ruth 1:2 The man's name was Elimelech, his wife was Naomi, and their two sons were Mahlon and Chilion, from Bethlehem in Judah. They went to live in the land of Moab and stayed there.
Ruth 1:3 Naomi's husband Elimelech died; she was left with her two sons.
Ruth 1:4 They married women from Moab; one was named Orpah and the other Ruth, and they lived there for about ten years.
Ruth 1:5 Mahlon and Chilion also died; the woman lost her two sons and her husband.
Ruth 1:6 Then she got up with her daughters-in-law to go back from Moab because she heard God had given food to his people there.
Ruth 1:7 So she left the place where she was, with her two daughters-in-law, and they traveled back to the land of Judah.
Ruth 1:8 Naomi told her two daughters-in-law, "Go back to your mothers' homes. May God be kind to you, just as you were to the ones who have died, and to me."
Ruth 1:9 May God help you find peace in your husbands' homes. Then she kissed them, and they all cried aloud.
Ruth 1:10 They told her, "We will definitely go back with you to your people."
Ruth 1:11 Naomi said, "Go back, my daughters. Why come with me? Do I have more sons in my belly to become your husbands?"
Ruth 1:12 Come back, my daughters, go on; because I am too old to get a husband. Even if I said I have hope, and even if I got a husband tonight, and then had sons;
Ruth 1:13 Would you wait for them until they grow up? Would you remain single for them? No, my daughters; it makes me very sad for you that God has turned against me.
Ruth 1:14 They cried out loud again, and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye; but Ruth stayed close to her.
Ruth 1:15 She said, "Look, your sister-in-law has returned to her people and her gods; you should go back after your sister-in-law."
Ruth 1:16 Ruth said, "Don't ask me to leave you or stop following you. Where you go, I will go; where you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God."
Ruth 1:17 Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May God do the same to me, and even more, if anything but death separates you and me.
Ruth 1:18 When she saw that she was determined to go with her, then she stopped talking to her.
Ruth 1:19 So they both went until they reached Bethlehem. When they got there, the whole town was stirred because of them, and they asked, "Is this Naomi?"
Ruth 1:20 She told them, "Don't call me Naomi, call me Mara, because God has made my life very bitter."
Ruth 1:21 I left with everything and God brought me back with nothing: why do you still call me Naomi when God has shown disapproval of me, and the Almighty has caused me suffering?
Ruth 1:22 Naomi went back, and with her went Ruth the Moabitess, her daughter-in-law, who had come from the country of Moab. They arrived in Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest.

Ruth 2:1 Naomi had a relative from her husband's family who was very wealthy, and his name was Boaz.
Ruth 2:2 Ruth from Moab said to Naomi, "Let me go to the fields to pick up leftover grain from someone who will show me kindness." Naomi replied, "Go ahead, my daughter."
Ruth 2:3 She went out, came, and picked up leftover grain in the field behind the harvesters. By chance, she ended up in a part of the field owned by Boaz, who was related to Elimelech.
Ruth 2:4 Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and said to the harvesters, "God be with you." They replied, "God bless you."
Ruth 2:5 Then Boaz asked his servant in charge of the harvesters, "Who is this young woman?"
Ruth 2:6 The worker in charge of the harvesters replied, "She is the young woman from Moab who returned with Naomi from the land of Moab."
Ruth 2:7 She said, "Please let me pick up leftover grain behind the harvesters among the bundles." So she went, and has been working from morning until now, except for a short rest in the shelter.
Ruth 2:8 Boaz said to Ruth, "Didn't you hear, my daughter? Don't go to pick grain in another field, or leave this place, but stay close to my women workers."
Ruth 2:9 Watch the field where they are harvesting, and follow them. Haven't I told the men not to bother you? When you're thirsty, go to the jars and drink what the men have filled.
Ruth 2:10 Then she knelt down, bowed to the ground, and said to him, "Why have I found favor in your eyes, that you notice me, even though I am a foreigner?"
Ruth 2:11 Boaz replied to her, "I've been told about everything you did for your mother-in-law after your husband died, and how you left your parents and your birthplace to come to a people you didn't know before."
Ruth 2:12 God repay your work, and may you get a full reward from the God of Israel, under whose protection you have come to trust.
Ruth 2:13 Then she said, "Please look on me with kindness, sir, because you have comforted me and spoken kindly to me, your servant, even though I am not like one of your maidservants."
Ruth 2:14 Boaz said to her, "Come here at mealtime, eat some bread, and dip your piece in the vinegar." She sat next to the harvesters, and he handed her some roasted grain. She ate, was satisfied, and had some left over.
Ruth 2:15 When she got up to collect grain, Boaz told his workers, "Let her gather grain even among the bundles, and do not bother her."
Ruth 2:16 Drop some extra grain for her on purpose and leave it so she can pick it up, and do not scold her.
Ruth 2:17 She picked grain in the field until evening, then she threshed what she had collected, and it was about an ephah of barley.
Ruth 2:18 She picked it up, went to the city, and her mother-in-law saw what she had gathered. She then brought out and gave to her the leftovers she had kept after eating enough.
Ruth 2:19 Her mother-in-law asked her, "Where did you gather grain today? Where did you work? May God bless the one who noticed you." Then she told her mother-in-law who she had worked with and said, "The man I worked with today is named Boaz."
Ruth 2:20 Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, "May God bless him for his kindness to both the living and the dead." Naomi also told her, "That man is one of our close relatives."
Ruth 2:21 Ruth, from Moab, said, "He also told me to stay close to his young men until they finish all his harvest."
Ruth 2:22 Naomi said to Ruth, her daughter-in-law, "It's good, my daughter, for you to go out with his young women, so that you are not met in any other field."
Ruth 2:23 She stayed close to Boaz's servant girls to pick grain until the barley and wheat harvests were finished; and she lived with her mother-in-law.

Ruth 3:1 Then Naomi, her mother-in-law, said to her, "My daughter, shouldn't I find a peaceful place for you, so you can be happy?"
Ruth 3:2 Isn't Boaz, who is related to us, the one whose young women you were with? Look, he is separating the barley on the threshing floor tonight.
Ruth 3:3 Clean yourself, then put on perfume and your clothes, and go to the threshing floor. But don't let the man see you until he has finished eating and drinking.
Ruth 3:4 When he lies down, notice where he is, then go, uncover his feet, lie down, and he will explain what you should do.
Ruth 3:5 She told her, "I will do everything you tell me to do."
Ruth 3:6 She went to the threshing floor and did everything her mother-in-law told her to.
Ruth 3:7 After Boaz finished eating and drinking, feeling happy, he went to sleep by the pile of grain. Then she quietly approached, uncovered his feet, and lay down.
Ruth 3:8 At midnight, the man became scared and turned around, and he saw a woman lying at his feet.
Ruth 3:9 He asked, "Who are you?" She replied, "I am Ruth, your servant. Please cover me with your cloak, because you are a close relative."
Ruth 3:10 He said, "You are blessed by God, my daughter, because you have shown more kindness now than before. You did not go after young men, whether they were poor or rich."
Ruth 3:11 Now, my daughter, do not be afraid; I will do all that you ask, because everyone in my town knows you are a good woman.
Ruth 3:12 It is true that I am one of your relatives, but there is another relative closer than me.
Ruth 3:13 Stay tonight, and in the morning, if he agrees to help you as a relative should, good; let him help. But if he does not want to help as a relative, then I will help you, as surely as God lives. Rest until morning.
Ruth 3:14 She stayed at his feet until morning, and she got up before anyone could recognize each other. And he said, "Don't let anyone know that a woman was here on the threshing floor."
Ruth 3:15 He also said, "Bring the veil you're wearing and hold it out." So when she did, he poured six scoops of barley into it and placed it on her back, then she went back to the city.
Ruth 3:16 When she went to her mother-in-law, she asked, "Who are you, my daughter?" And she explained everything the man had done to her.
Ruth 3:17 She said, "He gave me these six measures of barley and told me, 'Don't go to your mother-in-law empty-handed.'"
Ruth 3:18 She said, "Stay here, my daughter, until you find out what happens. The man won't rest until he sorts it out today."

Ruth 4:1 Boaz went to the town gate and sat down. Then the relative he had mentioned came by. Boaz called, "Come over here and sit down." So he came over and sat down.
Ruth 4:2 He took ten city elders and said, "Sit down here." And they sat down.
Ruth 4:3 He told the relative, "Naomi, who has returned from Moab, is selling a piece of land that belonged to our brother Elimelech."
Ruth 4:4 I planned to tell you, 'Buy it in front of the locals and the elders of our people. If you will buy it back, do it. But if you won’t, let me know, so I can know, because there's no one else to buy it back except you, and I’m next after you.' And he said, 'I'll buy it back.'
Ruth 4:5 Then Boaz said, "When you buy the field from Naomi, you must also buy it from Ruth the Moabite, the widow, to continue the name of the deceased on his property."
Ruth 4:6 The relative said, "I can't buy it for myself without harming my own inheritance. Take over my right to buy it, because I can't do it."
Ruth 4:7 In the past in Israel, when someone needed to confirm a deal about buying back or trading property, that person would take off his shoe and give it to the other person. This was how they showed the agreement was official in Israel.
Ruth 4:8 So the relative said to Boaz, "Buy it yourself." And he took off his shoe.
Ruth 4:9 Boaz said to the elders and all the people, "You are witnesses today that I have bought everything that belonged to Elimelech, and everything that belonged to Chilion and Mahlon, from Naomi."
Ruth 4:10 Also, I have bought Ruth the Moabite, Mahlon's widow, to be my wife. This is to keep the dead man's name alive with his property so that his name won't disappear among his family or from his hometown. You are all witnesses today.
Ruth 4:11 All the people and the elders at the gate said, "We are witnesses. May God make this woman coming into your home like Rachel and Leah, who together built the family of Israel. May you prosper in Ephratah and be well-known in Bethlehem."
Ruth 4:12 May your family be like the family of Pharez, whom Tamar had with Judah, from the children that God will give you with this young woman.
Ruth 4:13 So Boaz married Ruth, and she became his wife. When he was intimate with her, God allowed her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son.
Ruth 4:14 The women said to Naomi, "Praise God, who has given you a relative today to make his name known in Israel."
Ruth 4:15 He will restore your life and care for you in your old age, because your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is more precious to you than seven sons, has given birth to him.
Ruth 4:16 Naomi held the baby close to her and cared for it like a nurse.
Ruth 4:17 The women living nearby named the baby, saying, "Naomi has a son;" and they named him Obed. Obed became the father of Jesse, who was David's father.
Ruth 4:18 These are the descendants of Perez: Perez was the father of Hezron.
Ruth 4:19 Hezron had a son named Ram, and Ram had a son named Amminadab.
Ruth 4:20 Amminadab had Nahshon, and Nahshon had Salmon.
Ruth 4:21 Salmon was the father of Boaz, and Boaz was the father of Obed.
Ruth 4:22 Obed had Jesse, and Jesse had David.

1 Samuel 1:1 There was a man from Ramathaim, a town in the Ephraim hills, named Elkanah. He was Jeroham's son, Elihu's grandson, Tohu's great-grandson, and Zuph's great-great-grandson, from the tribe of Ephraim.
1 Samuel 1:2 He had two wives; one was named Hannah and the other Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah did not.
1 Samuel 1:3 This man went to his city every year to worship and offer sacrifices to God in Shiloh. Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, who were priests of God, were there.
1 Samuel 1:4 When it was time for Elkanah to make an offering, he gave portions to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters.
1 Samuel 1:5 But he gave Hannah a special share because he loved her, even though God had closed her womb.
1 Samuel 1:6 Her enemy upset her a lot to make her worry because God had closed her womb.
1 Samuel 1:7 Every year, when she went to God's house, she upset her. So she cried and didn't eat.
1 Samuel 1:8 Elkanah, her husband, said to her, "Hannah, why are you crying? Why aren't you eating? Why are you so sad? Aren't I more important to you than ten sons?"
1 Samuel 1:9 Hannah stood up after eating in Shiloh and after drinking. Eli the priest was sitting on a chair by the temple doorpost of God.
1 Samuel 1:10 She felt deep sadness, prayed to God, and cried hard.
1 Samuel 1:11 She made a promise and said, "God of all, if you truly see my suffering and remember me, and not forget me, but give me a son, then I will dedicate him to God for all his life, and his hair will never be cut."
1 Samuel 1:12 As she kept praying to God, Eli noticed her mouth moving.
1 Samuel 1:13 Hannah was praying silently; her lips moved but no sound came out, so Eli thought she was drunk.
1 Samuel 1:14 Eli asked her, "How long will you stay drunk? Stop drinking wine."
1 Samuel 1:15 Hannah replied, "No, sir, I am a woman with a sad heart. I haven't had wine or strong drink but have told all my troubles to God."
1 Samuel 1:16 Don't consider me a wicked woman, for I have spoken from deep sadness and frustration up to now.
1 Samuel 1:17 Eli answered and said, "Go in peace, and may the God of Israel give you what you have asked from Him."
1 Samuel 1:18 She said, "I hope I have been good in your eyes." So the woman left, ate, and was not sad anymore.
1 Samuel 1:19 They got up early in the morning, worshiped God, then went back to their home in Ramah. Elkanah was with his wife Hannah, and God remembered her.
1 Samuel 1:20 So when the time came after Hannah became pregnant, she gave birth to a son and named him Samuel, because she had asked God for him.
1 Samuel 1:21 Elkanah and his family went to give God their yearly sacrifice and to fulfill his promise.
1 Samuel 1:22 But Hannah didn't go; she told her husband, "I won't go until the child is done nursing. Then I'll take him to appear before God, and he will stay there always."
1 Samuel 1:23 Elkanah, her husband, said to her, "Do what you think is best; stay until you have finished breastfeeding him; may God make sure His promise comes true." So the woman stayed and breastfed her son until she stopped.
1 Samuel 1:24 After she stopped breastfeeding him, she brought him along with three young cows, some flour, and a bottle of wine to God's house in Shiloh; the boy was still little.
1 Samuel 1:25 They killed a bull and brought the boy to Eli.
1 Samuel 1:26 And she said, "Oh sir, as you are alive, sir, I am the woman who was standing here with you, praying to God."
1 Samuel 1:27 I prayed for this child, and God has granted what I asked of Him.
1 Samuel 1:28 So I have given him to God; for as long as he lives, he will be given to God. And he worshiped God there.

1 Samuel 2:1 Hannah prayed and said, "My heart is happy in God, I am strong in God; my words are bold over my enemies because I am glad for your rescue."
1 Samuel 2:2 No one is as holy as God; no one else is like you; no other is as strong as our God.
1 Samuel 2:3 Stop speaking so proudly and don't let arrogance come from your mouth; because God knows everything, and he judges what you do.
1 Samuel 2:4 The strong warriors' bows are broken, and those who tripped are now strong.
1 Samuel 2:5 People who had plenty now work for food; those who were hungry are not hungry anymore. So, the woman with no children has seven, and the woman with many children has grown weak.
1 Samuel 2:6 God can cause death or give life; He can send people to the grave and raise them up again.
1 Samuel 2:7 God makes some poor and others rich; He humbles some and elevates others.
1 Samuel 2:8 God raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the trash heap to seat them with nobles and to give them a glorious throne. The earth's foundations belong to God, and he has placed the world on them.
1 Samuel 2:9 God will protect his holy people, and the wicked will be quiet in the dark; no one will succeed by their own power.
1 Samuel 2:10 God's enemies will be shattered; He will thunder against them from heaven: God will judge the whole world; He will give power to his king and lift up the strength of his chosen one.
1 Samuel 2:11 Elkanah went home to Ramah, and the boy served God in the presence of Eli the priest.
1 Samuel 2:12 Eli's sons were bad men; they did not know God.
1 Samuel 2:13 When people offered a sacrifice, the priest's assistant would come with a three-pronged fork while the meat was boiling.
1 Samuel 2:14 He put it into the pan, kettle, cauldron, or pot; whatever the meat hook pulled out, the priest kept for himself. This is what they did in Shiloh to all the Israelites who came there.
1 Samuel 2:15 Before they burned the fat, the priest's helper came and told the person offering the sacrifice, "Give meat to cook for the priest; he doesn't want boiled meat from you, only uncooked."
1 Samuel 2:16 If someone told him, "Please burn the fat right away, and then take whatever you want," he would say, "No, give it to me now; if you don't, I'll take it by force."
1 Samuel 2:17 The young men's sin was very bad in God's sight because people hated God's offerings.
1 Samuel 2:18 Samuel served in front of God as a child, wearing a linen garment.
1 Samuel 2:19 His mother made him a small coat and brought it to him every year when she went with her husband to make the annual sacrifice.
1 Samuel 2:20 Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife, saying, "May God give you children from this woman to repay what was given to God." Then they went to their home.
1 Samuel 2:21 God blessed Hannah, and she became pregnant, giving birth to three sons and two daughters. The boy Samuel grew up in the presence of God.
1 Samuel 2:22 Eli was very old and knew what his sons were doing to all of Israel; he knew they slept with the women who gathered at the entrance of the meeting tent.
1 Samuel 2:23 He asked them, "Why are you doing these bad things? Everyone is talking about your evil actions."
1 Samuel 2:24 No, my sons; it is not a good thing I am told: you make God's people do wrong.
1 Samuel 2:25 If someone sins against another person, a judge will decide the case. But if someone sins against God, who will plead for them? Yet they did not listen to their father's warnings, for God intended to punish them.
1 Samuel 2:26 The boy Samuel grew up and was liked by both God and people.
1 Samuel 2:27 A man of God came to Eli and said to him, "This is what God says: Did I clearly show myself to your father's family when they were in Egypt, in Pharaoh's palace?"
1 Samuel 2:28 Did I pick him from all Israel’s tribes to be my priest, to give sacrifices on my altar, to burn incense, and to wear the ephod in my presence? And did I give your father's family all the Israelites' fire offerings?
1 Samuel 2:29 Why do you disrespect my sacrifice and the offerings I ordered in my dwelling, and favor your sons over me, getting rich from the best parts of the offerings of Israel, my people?
1 Samuel 2:30 So God, the God of Israel, says, 'I thought your family and your ancestors would always serve me, but now God declares, 'That will not happen because I will honor those who honor me, and I will not value those who look down on me.'
1 Samuel 2:31 Look, the time will come when I will end your family power, and no old man will remain in your family.
1 Samuel 2:32 You will see a rival in my home, in all the riches God gives Israel, and you will never have an old man in your family.
1 Samuel 2:33 The man from your family who I won't remove from serving at my altar will cause you sadness and pain, and all of your descendants will die young.
1 Samuel 2:34 This will be a sign for you: your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, will both die on the same day.
1 Samuel 2:35 I will choose a loyal priest who will do what I want and think. I will give him a strong family, and he will serve my chosen one forever.
1 Samuel 2:36 Everyone remaining in your family will approach him, bow down for some money and food, and will ask, "Please give me a priest's job so I can have some bread to eat."

1 Samuel 3:1 The boy Samuel served God with Eli. In those times, God's messages were rare and visions were not common.
1 Samuel 3:2 At that time, when Eli was lying down in his spot and his eyes were starting to grow weak so he couldn't see;
1 Samuel 3:3 Before the lamp of God went out in God's temple, where God's ark was, and Samuel had gone to bed;
1 Samuel 3:4 God called Samuel, and he answered, "I'm here."
1 Samuel 3:5 He ran to Eli and said, "Here I am; you called me." But Eli answered, "I didn't call; go back to bed." So he went and lay down again.
1 Samuel 3:6 God called Samuel again, and Samuel got up and went to Eli and said, "Here I am, you called me." But he replied, "I didn't call you, my son; go back to sleep."
1 Samuel 3:7 Samuel did not yet know God, and God's word had not been shown to him.
1 Samuel 3:8 God called Samuel a third time. He got up, went to Eli, and said, "I'm here; you called me." Then Eli realized that God had called the boy.
1 Samuel 3:9 So Eli told Samuel, "Go back to bed, and if he calls you, say, 'Speak, God; your servant is listening.'" Then Samuel went and lay down in his spot.
1 Samuel 3:10 God came, stood, and called as before, "Samuel, Samuel." Then Samuel answered, "Speak, for your servant is listening."
1 Samuel 3:11 God said to Samuel, "Look, I will do something in Israel that will make everyone's ears who hears it ring."
1 Samuel 3:12 On that day, I will do everything I said about Eli's family: when I start, I will finish it.
1 Samuel 3:13 I have told him that I will always judge his family for the wrongs he knows about; because his sons acted badly, and he did not stop them.
1 Samuel 3:14 So I promised Eli's family that their wrongs will never be forgiven by sacrifice or offering.
1 Samuel 3:15 Samuel lay until morning and opened the doors of God's house. Samuel was afraid to tell Eli about the vision.
1 Samuel 3:16 Then Eli called Samuel and said, "Samuel, my son." And he replied, "I'm here."
1 Samuel 3:17 He asked, "What did God tell you? Please, don't keep it from me. May God punish you if you hide anything he said from me."
1 Samuel 3:18 Samuel told him everything, and kept nothing from him. And he said, It is God: let him do what seems good to him.
1 Samuel 3:19 Samuel grew up, and God was with him, and made sure that all his words were effective.
1 Samuel 3:20 Everyone in Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, understood that Samuel was confirmed as a prophet of God.
1 Samuel 3:21 God appeared again in Shiloh because He showed Himself to Samuel in Shiloh through God's message.

1 Samuel 4:1 Samuel's message reached all of Israel. Israel went to fight the Philistines, setting up near Ebenezer, while the Philistines camped at Aphek.
1 Samuel 4:2 The Philistines lined up to fight Israel: and when the battle started, Israel was defeated by the Philistines: and they killed about four thousand soldiers on the battlefield.
1 Samuel 4:3 When the people returned to the camp, the leaders of Israel asked, "Why did God beat us today before the Philistines? Let's bring the ark of God's covenant from Shiloh to us, so that when it's with us, it can save us from our enemies."
1 Samuel 4:4 So the people sent to Shiloh to bring back the ark of God's covenant, which is kept between the cherubim. Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were with the ark of God's covenant.
1 Samuel 4:5 When God's covenant chest came into the camp, all Israel yelled loudly, and the ground echoed.
1 Samuel 4:6 When the Philistines heard the shouting, they asked, "What does this loud cheering in the Hebrews' camp mean?" Then they realized the Ark of God had arrived in the camp.
1 Samuel 4:7 The Philistines were scared because they said, "God has come into the camp." They said, "This is terrible for us! Because nothing like this has ever happened before."
1 Samuel 4:8 We are in trouble! Who will rescue us from these powerful gods? These are the gods that struck the Egyptians with many plagues in the desert.
1 Samuel 4:9 Be brave and act like men, you Philistines, so you won't become slaves to the Hebrews as they have been to you. Act like men and fight.
1 Samuel 4:10 The Philistines battled, Israel was defeated, and everyone ran away to their tents: many were killed, with thirty thousand Israeli soldiers dying.
1 Samuel 4:11 God's ark was captured; Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were killed.
1 Samuel 4:12 A man from Benjamin ran from the battle and reached Shiloh that day with torn clothes and dirt on his head.
1 Samuel 4:13 When he arrived, Eli was sitting on a chair by the road looking out, because he was worried about God's ark. When the man entered the city and shared the news, everyone in the city shouted.
1 Samuel 4:14 When Eli heard the loud crying, he asked, "What does this loud noise mean?" The man rushed in and told Eli.
1 Samuel 4:15 Eli was ninety-eight years old and his eyes were weak so he couldn't see.
1 Samuel 4:16 The man told Eli, "I am the one who escaped from the army today." Eli asked, "What happened, my son?"
1 Samuel 4:17 The messenger replied, "Israel has run away from the Philistines, there's been a huge killing of our people, your two sons Hophni and Phinehas are dead, and the Ark of God has been captured."
1 Samuel 4:18 When he spoke about the ark of God, he fell backwards from his chair by the gate, broke his neck, and died because he was old and heavy. He had led Israel for forty years.
1 Samuel 4:19 Phinehas' wife, who was expecting a baby soon, found out that the Ark of God had been captured, and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead. She knelt down and began to give birth because her labor pains started.
1 Samuel 4:20 As she was dying, the women around her told her, "Don't be afraid; you have given birth to a son." But she did not answer or pay attention.
1 Samuel 4:21 She called the baby Ichabod, saying, "Glory has left Israel, because God's ark was captured, and because of her father-in-law and her husband."
1 Samuel 4:22 She said, "The glory has left Israel because the Ark of God has been captured."

1 Samuel 5:1 The Philistines captured God's chest and moved it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
1 Samuel 5:2 When the Philistines captured the ark of God, they brought it into Dagon's temple and placed it next to Dagon.
1 Samuel 5:3 When the people of Ashdod got up the next morning, they saw Dagon had fallen face down on the ground before God's ark. They put Dagon back in his spot.
1 Samuel 5:4 When they got up the next morning, they saw that Dagon had fallen face down on the ground before God's ark; Dagon's head and both hands were cut off and lying on the doorstep, leaving only his body.
1 Samuel 5:5 So the priests of Dagon and anyone who enters Dagon's temple in Ashdod do not step on Dagon's doorway even now.
1 Samuel 5:6 God's hand was heavy on the people of Ashdod; he ruined them and struck them with tumors, both in Ashdod and its surrounding areas.
1 Samuel 5:7 When the people of Ashdod noticed this, they said, "The ark of Israel's God can't stay with us because his power is too much for us and for Dagon, our god."
1 Samuel 5:8 So they called together all the Philistine rulers and asked, "What should we do with the ark of the God of Israel?" They decided, "Take the ark of the God of Israel to Gath." Then they moved the ark of the God of Israel there.
1 Samuel 5:9 And it happened that after they moved it, God brought a terrible disaster upon the city. He struck the people, young and old, and they developed tumors in their private areas.
1 Samuel 5:10 So they sent God's ark to Ekron. When God's ark arrived in Ekron, the people of Ekron shouted, "They have brought the ark of Israel's God to us to kill us and our people."
1 Samuel 5:11 So they called all the leaders of the Philistines and said, "Send back the ark of the God of Israel, so it can return to where it belongs and not kill us and our people." There was fatal trouble all over the city; God's power was very strong there.
1 Samuel 5:12 The men who did not die were struck with tumors, and the city's cry reached up to heaven.

1 Samuel 6:1 The chest of God stayed in the land of the Philistines for seven months.
1 Samuel 6:2 The Philistines asked their priests and fortune-tellers, "What should we do with the ark of God? Tell us how to send it back to where it belongs."
1 Samuel 6:3 They said, "If you send back the ark of the God of Israel, don't send it empty. Instead, definitely send a guilt offering with it. Then you will be healed, and you will understand why he is still punishing you."
1 Samuel 6:4 They asked, "What should we give as a guilt offering to him?" They replied, "Five gold tumors and five gold mice, equal to the number of Philistine rulers, because the same disease struck all of you and your rulers."
1 Samuel 6:5 So you will make models of your tumors and of the mice that ruin the land; and you will honor the God of Israel. Maybe He will ease His grip on you, your gods, and your land.
1 Samuel 6:6 Why then do you make your hearts hard, like the Egyptians and Pharaoh did? When God showed them amazing things, didn't they let the people go, and they left?
1 Samuel 6:7 So now, build a new cart, and get two milk cows that have never worn a yoke. Hitch the cows to the cart, but take their calves back home away from them.
1 Samuel 6:8 Take God's ark and put it on the cart; put the gold offerings you're giving back for your wrongdoing in a box next to it; and then send it off so it can leave.
1 Samuel 6:9 Look and see if it returns to Bethshemesh in its own territory, then God has caused this terrible thing to us. But if not, then we will know it was not God who hurt us, it just happened by chance.
1 Samuel 6:10 The men followed the instructions; they took two milk cows, hitched them to the cart, and kept their calves inside at home.
1 Samuel 6:11 They put the ark of God on the cart, along with the box containing the gold mice and the statues of their tumors.
1 Samuel 6:12 The cows went straight on the road to Bethshemesh, walking on the main road and mooing as they walked, not turning right or left; and the Philistine leaders followed them to the border of Bethshemesh.
1 Samuel 6:13 The people of Bethshemesh were cutting their wheat in the valley. They looked up, saw the ark, and were happy to see it.
1 Samuel 6:14 The cart arrived in Joshua's field, a man from Beth-shemesh, and stopped by a big stone. They cut up the cart's wood and used it to make a fire to burn the cows as an offering to God.
1 Samuel 6:15 The Levites moved God's chest and the box that was with it, which held the gold jewels, and placed them on a large rock. That day, the people of Bethshemesh offered burnt gifts and sacrifices to God.
1 Samuel 6:16 When the five Philistine leaders saw it, they went back to Ekron that day.
1 Samuel 6:17 These are the gold tumors the Philistines gave as a guilt offering to God: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron.
1 Samuel 6:18 The gold mice matched the number of all the Philistine cities governed by the five rulers, including walled cities and villages, up to the large stone of Abel, where they placed God's ark. This stone is still in Joshua the Bethshemite's field today.
1 Samuel 6:19 God punished the men of Bethshemesh for looking inside the ark of God, killing 50,070 of them, and the people mourned because God had struck down many with a great loss of life.
1 Samuel 6:20 The people of Bethshemesh asked, "Who can stand before this holy God? And who will He leave us to go to?"
1 Samuel 6:21 They sent messengers to the people of Kirjathjearim to say, "The Philistines have returned the ark of God; come and take it to your place."

1 Samuel 7:1 The men from Kirjathjearim came, took the ark of God, and brought it to Abinadab's house on the hill. They set apart Eleazar, his son, to take care of the ark of God.
1 Samuel 7:2 While the ark stayed in Kirjathjearim, a lot of time passed; it was twenty years: and all the people of Israel felt sad and missed God.
1 Samuel 7:3 Samuel spoke to all Israel and said, "If you truly come back to God with all your hearts, get rid of the foreign gods and Ashtaroth, make your hearts right with God, and serve only him, then he will save you from the Philistines."
1 Samuel 7:4 Then the Israelites stopped worshiping Baal and Ashtaroth and served only God.
1 Samuel 7:5 Samuel said, "Bring all of Israel to Mizpeh, and I will pray to God for you."
1 Samuel 7:6 They came together at Mizpeh, took water, poured it out before God, fasted that day, and said, "We have sinned against God." And Samuel decided cases for the Israelites in Mizpeh.
1 Samuel 7:7 When the Philistines found out that the Israelites had come together at Mizpeh, the Philistine rulers attacked Israel. The Israelites were scared when they heard this.
1 Samuel 7:8 The people of Israel told Samuel, "Don't stop praying to God for us, so that he will save us from the Philistines."
1 Samuel 7:9 Samuel took a young lamb and gave it as a complete burnt offering to God. Samuel prayed to God for Israel, and God listened to him.
1 Samuel 7:10 While Samuel was making the burnt offering, the Philistines came close to fight Israel: but God made a loud thunder that day on the Philistines, and confused them; and they were defeated by Israel.
1 Samuel 7:11 The Israelite men left Mizpeh, chased the Philistines, and defeated them all the way to Bethcar.
1 Samuel 7:12 Then Samuel took a stone, placed it between Mizpeh and Shen, and named it Ebenezer, saying, "Up to now, God has helped us."
1 Samuel 7:13 The Philistines were defeated and stopped entering Israel's territory; God opposed the Philistines during Samuel's entire life.
1 Samuel 7:14 The cities that the Philistines took from Israel were given back to Israel, from Ekron to Gath. Israel took them back from the Philistines. And Israel and the Amorites were at peace.
1 Samuel 7:15 Samuel was the judge of Israel all his life.
1 Samuel 7:16 He traveled every year to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpeh, and in all these places, he judged Israel.
1 Samuel 7:17 He went back to Ramah where his home was; there he decided cases for Israel and built an altar to God.

1 Samuel 8:1 When Samuel got old, he appointed his sons as judges for Israel.
1 Samuel 8:2 His first son was named Joel and his second, Abiah; they were judges in Beersheba.
1 Samuel 8:3 His sons did not follow his ways, but chased after money, accepted bribes, and twisted justice.
1 Samuel 8:4 All the leaders of Israel came together and went to see Samuel in Ramah.
1 Samuel 8:5 They said to him, "Look, you are old and your sons do not follow your ways. Now appoint for us a king to lead us, like other nations have."
1 Samuel 8:6 Samuel was upset when they said, "Give us a king to lead us." So he prayed to God.
1 Samuel 8:7 God said to Samuel, "Listen to what the people are saying to you. They haven't rejected you; they've rejected me as their ruler."
1 Samuel 8:8 Based on everything they've done since I took them out of Egypt until now, they have left me and worshiped other gods; they are doing the same to you.
1 Samuel 8:9 Listen to what they say, but clearly warn them and explain how the king who will rule them will act.
1 Samuel 8:10 Samuel told the people who wanted a king everything that God had said.
1 Samuel 8:11 He said, "The king who will rule over you will take your sons for himself, to use them for his chariots and as his horsemen, and some will run in front of his chariots."
1 Samuel 8:12 He will make people leaders over groups of a thousand and leaders over groups of fifty; he will assign them to plow his land, harvest his crops, and make his weapons and chariot equipment.
1 Samuel 8:13 He will take your daughters to make sweets, to cook, and to bake.
1 Samuel 8:14 He will take your farms, grapevines, and olive groves, the best ones, and give them to his workers.
1 Samuel 8:15 He will take a tenth of your crops and your vineyards and give it to his officials and servants.
1 Samuel 8:16 He will take your male and female servants, your best young men, and your donkeys, and make them work for him.
1 Samuel 8:17 He will take a tenth of your sheep, and you will become his servants.
1 Samuel 8:18 You will cry out on that day because of the king you chose; but God will not listen to you on that day.
1 Samuel 8:19 Still, the people wouldn't listen to Samuel, saying, "No, we want a king to rule over us."
1 Samuel 8:20 We want to be like other countries; we want our king to make decisions for us, lead us, and fight our wars.
1 Samuel 8:21 Samuel heard everything the people said and told it to God.
1 Samuel 8:22 God told Samuel, "Listen to what they say and give them a king." Then Samuel said to the Israelites, "Everyone go back to your own town."

1 Samuel 9:1 There was a man from the tribe of Benjamin named Kish. He was the son of Abiel, the grandson of Zeror, the great-grandson of Bechorath, and the great-great-grandson of Aphiah. He was a strong and influential man.
1 Samuel 9:2 He had a son named Saul, a fine young man and handsome. There was no one more handsome in Israel than him. He was taller than everyone else from the shoulders up.
1 Samuel 9:3 Kish, Saul's dad, lost his donkeys. Kish told Saul, his son, "Take a servant with you, get up, and go find the donkeys."
1 Samuel 9:4 He went through the hills of Ephraim and the area of Shalisha, but they didn't find them. Then they went through the area of Shalim, and they weren't there either. He also went through the land of Benjamin, but still, they didn't find them.
1 Samuel 9:5 When they reached the land of Zuph, Saul told his servant with him, "Let's go back, or my father will stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about us."
1 Samuel 9:6 He told him, "Look, in this city there's a man of God who is respected; everything he says happens for sure. Let's go there; maybe he can tell us the way we should take."
1 Samuel 9:7 Then Saul said to his servant, "But if we go, what can we give the man? Our food is gone, and we don't have a gift for the man of God. What do we have?"
1 Samuel 9:8 The servant told Saul again, "Look, I have a quarter of a silver coin here. I will give it to the man of God to show us the way."
1 Samuel 9:9 Before in Israel, when someone wanted to ask God something, they would say, "Let's go to the seer." What we now call a Prophet was once called a Seer.
1 Samuel 9:10 Saul told his servant, "Good idea; let's go." So they set off towards the city where the man of God lived.
1 Samuel 9:11 As they climbed the hill to the city, they met young women going to get water and asked them, "Is the prophet here?"
1 Samuel 9:12 They replied, "Yes, he is here; he's just ahead of you. Hurry now, because he arrived in the city today since there's a people's sacrifice happening today at the high place."
1 Samuel 9:13 As soon as you arrive in the city, you will immediately find him before he goes up to eat at the high place, because the people won't eat until he arrives to bless the sacrifice. Then, those who are invited will eat. So go now; you will find him at this time.
1 Samuel 9:14 They went up to the city, and as they arrived, they saw Samuel coming out to meet them on his way to the worship place.
1 Samuel 9:15 God had told Samuel the day before Saul arrived, saying,
1 Samuel 9:16 Tomorrow at this time, I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you will anoint him as leader over my people Israel, so he can save them from the Philistines; because I have heard my people's cry for help.
1 Samuel 9:17 When Samuel saw Saul, God told him, "Look at the man I told you about! He will rule over my people."
1 Samuel 9:18 Saul came close to Samuel at the gate and asked, "Please tell me where the prophet's house is."
1 Samuel 9:19 Samuel replied to Saul, "I am the prophet. Go ahead of me to the worship place; you will eat with me today, and tomorrow I will let you go and explain everything you are wondering about."
1 Samuel 9:20 Don't worry about your donkeys that went missing three days ago; they've been found. And who does all of Israel look up to? Isn't it you and your family?
1 Samuel 9:21 Saul replied, "Aren't I from Benjamin, the smallest tribe of Israel, and isn't my family the least important of all the families in the tribe of Benjamin? So why are you saying this to me?"
1 Samuel 9:22 Samuel took Saul and his servant to the dining room and had them sit in the best place among the about thirty invited guests.
1 Samuel 9:23 Samuel told the cook, "Bring the piece I gave you, the one I told you to keep aside."
1 Samuel 9:24 The cook picked up the shoulder meat and everything on it, and placed it in front of Saul. Then Samuel said, "Look, this is what's left! Put it in front of you and eat. It has been saved for you since I invited the people." So Saul ate with Samuel that day.
1 Samuel 9:25 After they came down from the high place to the city, Samuel talked with Saul on the roof of the house.
1 Samuel 9:26 They got up early. When the day began to dawn, Samuel called Saul to the rooftop and said, "Get up, so I can send you off." Saul got up, and they both went outside, Saul and Samuel.
1 Samuel 9:27 As they were walking to the edge of the city, Samuel told Saul, "Tell the servant to go ahead of us," (and he went ahead), "but you stay here for a moment, so I can tell you what God has to say."

1 Samuel 10:1 Then Samuel took a bottle of oil, poured it on his head, kissed him, and said, "Isn't it because God has chosen you to lead his people?"
1 Samuel 10:2 When you leave me today, you will meet two men near Rachel's tomb on Benjamin's border at Zelzah; they will tell you that the donkeys you were looking for have been found, and look, your father has stopped worrying about the donkeys and is now worried about you, wondering, 'What should I do for my son?'
1 Samuel 10:3 Then you will move on from there and reach Tabor's plain, where three men going to worship God at Bethel will meet you. One will have three young goats, another three loaves of bread, and the third a container of wine.
1 Samuel 10:4 They will greet you and give you two loaves of bread; you should take them from their hands.
1 Samuel 10:5 After that, you will go to God's hill, where the Philistine soldiers are: and when you get there, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the worship place with a psaltery, a tambourine, a flute, and a harp in front of them; and they will speak God's messages.
1 Samuel 10:6 God's Spirit will come on you, and you will prophesy with them, and you will be changed into a different person.
1 Samuel 10:7 When these signs happen to you, do what you think is best because God is with you.
1 Samuel 10:8 Go ahead of me to Gilgal, and wait there. I will come to you to offer burnt sacrifices and peace offerings. Stay for seven days until I arrive and tell you what to do.
1 Samuel 10:9 When he left Samuel and turned away, God changed his heart, and all the signs happened that day.
1 Samuel 10:10 When they got to the hill, a group of prophets met him; God's Spirit came on him, and he spoke God's messages with them.
1 Samuel 10:11 When everyone who knew him before saw that he was prophesying with the prophets, they asked each other, "What has happened to Kish's son? Is Saul also one of the prophets?"
1 Samuel 10:12 Someone from there replied, "But who is their father?" So it became a saying, "Is Saul also a prophet?"
1 Samuel 10:13 After he finished prophesying, he arrived at the high place.
1 Samuel 10:14 Saul's uncle asked him and his servant, "Where did you go?" He replied, "To look for the donkeys. When we couldn't find them anywhere, we went to Samuel."
1 Samuel 10:15 Saul's uncle asked, "Please tell me what Samuel said to you."
1 Samuel 10:16 Saul told his uncle, "He clearly said that the donkeys were found. But he didn't tell him about the kingdom business that Samuel mentioned."
1 Samuel 10:17 And Samuel gathered the people to God at Mizpeh.
1 Samuel 10:18 God told the people of Israel, "I took Israel out of Egypt, and saved you from the Egyptians and from every kingdom that pressured you."
1 Samuel 10:19 Today, you have turned away from God, who rescued you from all your troubles and hardships; and you have told Him, 'No, we want a king to rule over us.' So now, come stand before God by your tribes and in groups of a thousand.
1 Samuel 10:20 When Samuel had all Israel's tribes come forward, the tribe of Benjamin was chosen.
1 Samuel 10:21 When he made the tribe of Benjamin approach by their families, Matri's family was chosen, and Saul, Kish's son, was selected: but when they looked for him, he was not found.
1 Samuel 10:22 So they asked God again if the man would come there. And God said, "Look, he has hidden himself among the baggage."
1 Samuel 10:23 They hurried to get him from there, and when he stood with the people, he was taller than anyone else from his shoulders up.
1 Samuel 10:24 And Samuel said to everyone, "Look at the man whom God has chosen, there is no one like him among all the people." And all the people yelled, "God save the king."
1 Samuel 10:25 Samuel explained to the people how the kingdom should work, wrote it in a book, and put it before God. Then Samuel sent everyone home.
1 Samuel 10:26 Saul went back to Gibeah, and a group of men whose hearts God had moved went with him.
1 Samuel 10:27 But Belial's followers said, "How can this man save us?" They looked down on him and gave him no gifts. But he stayed quiet.

1 Samuel 11:1 Then Nahash the Ammonite arrived and camped against Jabeshgilead. All the men of Jabesh told Nahash, "Make an agreement with us, and we will serve you."
1 Samuel 11:2 Nahash the Ammonite replied, "I will make an agreement with you only if I can gouge out everyone's right eye, to shame all of Israel."
1 Samuel 11:3 The leaders of Jabesh said to him, "Give us seven days to send messengers throughout Israel for help. If no one comes to rescue us, we will surrender to you."
1 Samuel 11:4 The messengers arrived at Saul's Gibeah and told the news to the people; everyone cried out loud and wept.
1 Samuel 11:5 Saul returned from the fields, following the herd. He asked, "Why are the people crying?" They told him what happened to the men of Jabesh.
1 Samuel 11:6 God's Spirit came over Saul when he heard the news, and he became very angry.
1 Samuel 11:7 He took a pair of oxen, cut them up, and sent the pieces throughout Israel by messengers, saying, "Whoever doesn't follow Saul and Samuel will have their oxen treated the same way." The people were afraid of God and agreed to come together.
1 Samuel 11:8 When he counted them in Bezek, the Israelites were 300,000, and the men of Judah were 30,000.
1 Samuel 11:9 They told the messengers, "Say to the men of Jabeshgilead, 'By tomorrow, when the sun is hot, you will get help.'" The messengers told the men of Jabesh, and they were happy.
1 Samuel 11:10 So the men of Jabesh told them, "Tomorrow we will surrender to you, and you can do to us whatever you think is right."
1 Samuel 11:11 The next day, Saul divided the people into three groups. They attacked the enemy camp during the early morning and fought the Ammonites until it was hot. The remaining Ammonites ran away, and not even two of them stayed together.
1 Samuel 11:12 The people said to Samuel, "Who questioned whether Saul would rule over us? Bring those men so we can kill them."
1 Samuel 11:13 Saul said, "No one will be killed today because God has given Israel victory today."
1 Samuel 11:14 Samuel told the people, "Come, let's go to Gilgal and start the kingdom again there."
1 Samuel 11:15 All the people went to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before God. They offered peace sacrifices to God in Gilgal, and Saul and all the Israelite men were very happy.

1 Samuel 12:1 Samuel told all of Israel, "Look, I have listened to what you said to me, and I have made a king for you."
1 Samuel 12:2 Now look, the king leads you. I am old with gray hair, and my sons are with you. I have led you from my youth until now.
1 Samuel 12:3 Look, I am here: speak against me before God, and his chosen leader: Which ox or donkey have I taken? Who have I cheated or treated unfairly? From whom have I taken a bribe to look the other way? Tell me and I will give it back.
1 Samuel 12:4 They said, "You have not cheated or mistreated us, nor have you taken anything from anyone."
1 Samuel 12:5 He told them, "God is your witness, and his chosen one is also a witness today, that you found nothing wrong in what I've done." And they replied, "He is our witness."
1 Samuel 12:6 Samuel told the people, "It is God who promoted Moses and Aaron, and who led your ancestors out of Egypt."
1 Samuel 12:7 Now stand still so I can tell you about all the good things God did for you and your ancestors.
1 Samuel 12:8 When Jacob arrived in Egypt, and your ancestors called out to God, then God sent Moses and Aaron who led your ancestors out of Egypt and settled them here.
1 Samuel 12:9 When they forgot God, he let Sisera, the army leader of Hazor, the Philistines, and the king of Moab capture them and fight against them.
1 Samuel 12:10 They called out to God, saying, "We have sinned by leaving God and serving Baal and Ashtaroth. Now save us from our enemies, and we will serve you."
1 Samuel 12:11 God sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel, and saved you from your enemies all around, and you lived in safety.
1 Samuel 12:12 When you saw that King Nahash of the Ammonites was attacking, you told me, 'No, we want a king to rule over us,' even though God was already your king.
1 Samuel 12:13 Now see the king you chose and wanted! God has made him your king.
1 Samuel 12:14 If you respect God, serve Him, listen to His words, and don't disobey His commands, then both you and the king who rules over you will keep on following God.
1 Samuel 12:15 But if you don't listen to God's voice and disobey His command, then God will be against you, just as He was against your ancestors.
1 Samuel 12:16 Now stand and watch this amazing thing that God will do before you.
1 Samuel 12:17 Isn't it wheat harvest today? I will call to God, and he will make thunder and rain come; so you will realize and see how bad your wrongdoings are, which you did before God by asking for a king.
1 Samuel 12:18 So Samuel prayed to God, and God made thunder and rain that day; and all the people were very afraid of God and Samuel.
1 Samuel 12:19 And all the people told Samuel, "Pray for us to God that we don't die, because we have made our sins worse by asking for a king."
1 Samuel 12:20 Samuel told the people, "Don't be afraid. You have done wrong, but do not stop following God. Instead, serve God with all your heart."
1 Samuel 12:21 Do not turn away: if you do, you will chase worthless things that cannot help or save you, because they are useless.
1 Samuel 12:22 God will not abandon his people for the sake of his great name: because it has pleased God to make you his people.
1 Samuel 12:23 Also, I would never sin against God by stopping my prayers for you. Instead, I will show you the good and right way to live.
1 Samuel 12:24 Only be afraid of God, and serve Him honestly with all your heart: for think about the amazing things He has done for you.
1 Samuel 12:25 If you keep doing bad things, you and your king will be destroyed.

1 Samuel 13:1 Saul was king for one year; after two years as king of Israel,
1 Samuel 13:2 Saul picked 3,000 Israeli soldiers; 2,000 stayed with Saul in Michmash and Bethel, 1,000 were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin, and he sent the others home.
1 Samuel 13:3 Jonathan attacked the Philistine outpost at Geba, and the Philistines found out. Saul sounded the trumpet all over the country, saying, "Let the Israelites hear."
1 Samuel 13:4 Everyone in Israel heard that Saul had defeated a Philistine outpost, and that the Philistines hated Israel. So the people gathered to follow Saul to Gilgal.
1 Samuel 13:5 The Philistines came together to battle Israel with thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and a huge crowd like the sand by the sea. They advanced and set up camp at Michmash, to the east of Bethaven.
1 Samuel 13:6 When the Israelite men realized they were in trouble because the people were distressed, they hid in caves, bushes, rocks, high areas, and pits.
1 Samuel 13:7 Some Hebrews crossed the Jordan River to Gad and Gilead, while Saul was still in Gilgal, and all the people with him were scared.
1 Samuel 13:8 He waited seven days, as Samuel had ordered, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal; and the people left him.
1 Samuel 13:9 Saul said, "Bring me a burnt offering and peace offerings." Then he gave the burnt offering.
1 Samuel 13:10 After he finished the burnt offering, Samuel arrived; Saul went out to greet him.
1 Samuel 13:11 And Samuel asked, "What have you done?" Saul answered, "I saw the people leaving me, you didn't arrive when you said you would, and the Philistines were uniting at Michmash."
1 Samuel 13:12 So I thought, 'The Philistines will soon attack me at Gilgal, and I haven't asked for God's help.' So I felt I had to go ahead and offer a sacrifice.
1 Samuel 13:13 Samuel said to Saul, "You have acted foolishly; you did not follow God's command which He gave you. Because of this, God would have made your rule over Israel last forever, but now he will not."
1 Samuel 13:14 But now your kingdom won't last. God has chosen a man who pleases Him, and God has told him to lead His people because you did not follow God's commands.
1 Samuel 13:15 Samuel got up and went from Gilgal to Gibeah in Benjamin. Saul counted the people with him, about six hundred men.
1 Samuel 13:16 Saul, his son Jonathan, and the people with them stayed in Gibeah in Benjamin's land, while the Philistines camped in Michmash.
1 Samuel 13:17 The raiders came out of the Philistines' camp in three groups: one group went toward the road to Ophrah, in Shual's territory.
1 Samuel 13:18 One group went towards Bethhoron, and another went along the road that borders the valley of Zeboim, heading to the desert.
1 Samuel 13:19 In all of Israel, no blacksmith could be found because the Philistines didn't want the Hebrews to make swords or spears.
1 Samuel 13:20 All the Israelites went to the Philistines to sharpen their plows, cutting tools, axes, and hoes.
1 Samuel 13:21 They had a tool to sharpen the hoes, plows, forks, axes, and prods.
1 Samuel 13:22 On the battle day, no one with Saul and Jonathan had a sword or spear, except for Saul and his son Jonathan.
1 Samuel 13:23 The Philistine soldiers went to the Michmash path.

1 Samuel 14:1 One day, Jonathan, Saul's son, told his armor-bearer, "Come, let's go to the Philistine camp on the other side." But he didn't tell his father.
1 Samuel 14:2 Saul waited at the edge of Gibeah under a pomegranate tree in Migron, and there were about six hundred men with him.
1 Samuel 14:3 Ahiah, Ahitub's son, Ichabod's brother, Phinehas's son, Eli's son, God's priest in Shiloh, wore an ephod. The people didn't know Jonathan had left.
1 Samuel 14:4 Between the paths where Jonathan wanted to cross to the Philistines' camp, there was a steep cliff on one side and a steep cliff on the other side. One cliff was called Bozez, and the other was called Seneh.
1 Samuel 14:5 The front of one was positioned to the north facing Michmash, and the other to the south facing Gibeah.
1 Samuel 14:6 Jonathan said to his armor bearer, "Come, let's go to the camp of these uncircumcised men. Maybe God will help us, because God can save with a lot or a few."
1 Samuel 14:7 His helper said to him, "Do all that is in your heart: go ahead; see, I am with you, as you feel in your heart."
1 Samuel 14:8 Jonathan said, "Look, we will go over to these men and show ourselves to them."
1 Samuel 14:9 If they tell us, 'Wait here until we come to you,' then we'll stay where we are and not go up to them.
1 Samuel 14:10 But if they say, "Come up to us," then we will go up, because God has given them into our hands, and this will be a sign to us.
1 Samuel 14:11 Both of them showed themselves to the Philistine outpost, and the Philistines said, "Look, the Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they were hiding."
1 Samuel 14:12 The soldiers at the fort called out to Jonathan and his helper, "Come up to us, and we'll teach you a lesson." Jonathan then said to his helper, "Follow me up, because God has given them to Israel's power."
1 Samuel 14:13 Jonathan climbed up using his hands and feet, and his armor-bearer followed him. The enemies fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer killed them after he did.
1 Samuel 14:14 Jonathan and his helper killed about twenty men in an area as big as half an acre of land that a pair of oxen could plow.
1 Samuel 14:15 There was shaking in the army, in the field, and among all the people. The guards and the raiders were also afraid, and the ground shook very much.
1 Samuel 14:16 Saul's guards in Gibeah of Benjamin looked, and saw the crowd disappearing and they were attacking each other.
1 Samuel 14:17 Saul said to his men, "Count and see who is missing from us." After they counted, they saw that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not there.
1 Samuel 14:18 Saul said to Ahiah, "Bring the ark of God here," because the ark was with the Israelites then.
1 Samuel 14:19 While Saul was talking to the priest, the noise from the Philistine army grew louder and louder, so Saul told the priest to stop.
1 Samuel 14:20 Saul and all his followers gathered and went to fight. Suddenly, each man attacked the others, causing great confusion.
1 Samuel 14:21 The Hebrews who had joined the Philistines earlier and had gone with them to their camp from the surrounding area also switched sides to join the Israelites with Saul and Jonathan.
1 Samuel 14:22 Also, all the Israelite men who had hidden in the hills of Ephraim joined the chase when they heard the Philistines were running away.
1 Samuel 14:23 God saved Israel that day, and the battle moved to Bethaven.
1 Samuel 14:24 The Israelite men were upset that day because Saul had made the people promise, saying, “May the man who eats any food before evening, when I get revenge on my enemies, be cursed." So, no one ate anything all day.
1 Samuel 14:25 Everyone in the country went to a forest, and there was honey on the ground.
1 Samuel 14:26 When the people entered the forest, they saw honey dripping, but no one ate any because they were afraid of the promise they had made.
1 Samuel 14:27 Jonathan did not hear when his father ordered the people to make the promise. So he reached out with his stick, dipped it into a honeycomb, and tasted the honey; then his eyes brightened.
