2 Samuel 3:35 When everyone came to get David to eat before evening, David vowed, "May God deal with me, and even more, if I eat bread or anything else before the sun sets."
2 Samuel 3:36 Everyone saw what happened, and they liked it; just as everything the king did made the people happy.
2 Samuel 3:37 Everyone and all of Israel knew that day that the king did not want to kill Abner, Ner's son.
2 Samuel 3:38 The king told his servants, "Don't you know that today a prince and a great man has fallen in Israel?"
2 Samuel 3:39 Today, even though I am the anointed king, I am weak, and these sons of Zeruiah are too strong for me. God will pay back those who do evil for their wickedness.

2 Samuel 4:1 When Saul's son learned that Abner had died in Hebron, he felt weak, and all the Israelites were upset.
2 Samuel 4:2 Saul's son had two men who led groups: one was named Baanah and the other Rechab. They were sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, which was part of the Benjamin tribe.
2 Samuel 4:3 The people from Beeroth ran away to Gittaim and have lived there until now.
2 Samuel 4:4 Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son who could not walk. He was five years old when news of Saul and Jonathan's deaths came from Jezreel. His nurse picked him up and ran away. While she hurriedly fled, he fell and hurt his feet. His name was Mephibosheth.
2 Samuel 4:5 Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, went to Ishbosheth's house during the hottest part of the day while he was resting on his bed.
2 Samuel 4:6 They arrived at the center of the house pretending to collect wheat and then they stabbed him below the fifth rib, and Rechab with his brother Baanah got away.
2 Samuel 4:7 When they entered the house, he was lying on his bed in his bedroom. They hit him, killed him, and cut off his head. Then they took his head and escaped across the fields all night.
2 Samuel 4:8 They brought Ishbosheth's head to David in Hebron and told the king, "Here is the head of Ishbosheth, Saul's son, your enemy who wanted to kill you. God has taken revenge for you today against Saul and his family."
2 Samuel 4:9 David replied to Rechab and his brother Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, "As God lives, who has saved me from all trouble,
2 Samuel 4:10 Someone told me, 'Saul is dead.' He thought he was bringing good news, so I grabbed him and killed him in Ziklag because he expected a reward for his news.
2 Samuel 4:11 How much worse it is when evil men kill a good person in his own home on his bed? Will I not demand you pay for his death and remove you from the world?
2 Samuel 4:12 David ordered his men, and they killed them, cut off their hands and feet, and hung them by the pool in Hebron. However, they took Ishbosheth's head and buried it in Abner's tomb in Hebron.

2 Samuel 5:1 All the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, "Look, we are your own flesh and blood."
2 Samuel 5:2 Before, when Saul was our king, you were the one who led Israel out and in. And God told you, 'You will take care of my people Israel, and you will be their leader.'
2 Samuel 5:3 All the leaders of Israel went to see the king at Hebron. There, David made an agreement with them in Hebron before God, and they made David king over Israel.
2 Samuel 5:4 David was thirty when he became king, and he ruled for forty years.
2 Samuel 5:5 He ruled over Judah in Hebron for seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem, he ruled over all Israel and Judah for thirty-three years.
2 Samuel 5:6 The king and his men went to Jerusalem to meet the Jebusites who lived there. The Jebusites told David, "You can't come in here unless you get rid of the blind and lame people." They thought, "David can't come in here."
2 Samuel 5:7 David captured the fortress of Zion, which is now called the city of David.
2 Samuel 5:8 David said that day, "Whoever climbs through the water shaft and defeats the Jebusites, including the blind and lame whom David dislikes, will become the leader." That's why people say, "The blind and lame cannot enter the house."
2 Samuel 5:9 David lived in the fortress and named it David's city. He then built it up from the Millo and inside.
2 Samuel 5:10 David continued to become powerful, and God was with him.
2 Samuel 5:11 Hiram, king of Tyre, sent messengers to David with cedar trees, carpenters, and masons, and they built a house for David.
2 Samuel 5:12 David realized that God had made him king over Israel, and that God had lifted up his kingdom for the benefit of the people of Israel.
2 Samuel 5:13 David married more women and added them to his other wives in Jerusalem after he left Hebron, and he had more sons and daughters.
2 Samuel 5:14 Here are the names of his children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammuah, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon.
2 Samuel 5:15 Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, and Japhia were also there.
2 Samuel 5:16 Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphalet.
2 Samuel 5:17 When the Philistines learned that David had been made king over Israel, they all went to look for David; and when David heard about it, he went to the fortress.
2 Samuel 5:18 The Philistines came and scattered throughout the valley of Rephaim.
2 Samuel 5:19 David asked God, "Should I go to fight the Philistines? Will you give them to me?" God said to David, "Go, because I will surely give the Philistines to you."
2 Samuel 5:20 David came to Baalperazim, David defeated them there, and said, "God has burst through my enemies before me, like a flood." So he named that place Baalperazim.
2 Samuel 5:21 There they left their idols, and David and his men burned them.
2 Samuel 5:22 The Philistines came again and spread out in Rephaim Valley.
2 Samuel 5:23 When David asked God, He said, "Do not attack them straight on; instead, go around them and surprise them near the mulberry trees."
2 Samuel 5:24 When you hear a sound like marching in the tops of the mulberry trees, act quickly, for that means God is going ahead of you to defeat the Philistine army.
2 Samuel 5:25 David did as God had commanded him and struck down the Philistines from Geba to Gazer.

2 Samuel 6:1 David brought together thirty thousand select men of Israel again.
2 Samuel 6:2 David got up and went with everyone from Baale of Judah to move the ark of God with the name called God of the armies who lives among the cherubim.
2 Samuel 6:3 They placed God's ark on a new cart and took it from Abinadab's house in Gibeah. Abinadab's sons, Uzzah and Ahio, guided the new cart.
2 Samuel 6:4 They took it from Abinadab's house in Gibeah, going with God's box, and Ahio walked in front of it.
2 Samuel 6:5 David and everyone from Israel made music for God with all kinds of wooden instruments, like harps, lyres, drums, flutes, and cymbals.
2 Samuel 6:6 When they reached Nachon's threshing floor, Uzzah reached out to the Ark of God and grabbed it because the oxen stumbled.
2 Samuel 6:7 God became very angry with Uzzah and struck him down because of his mistake, and Uzzah died there next to the ark of God.
2 Samuel 6:8 David was upset because God had punished Uzzah, and he named that place Perezuzzah, which it is still called today.
2 Samuel 6:9 David was scared of God that day and asked, "How can the ark of God come to me?"
2 Samuel 6:10 So David did not take God's chest to his city, but he took it to the house of Obededom from Gath.
2 Samuel 6:11 The chest of God stayed in the home of Obededom the Gittite for three months, and God blessed Obededom and his whole family.
2 Samuel 6:12 Someone told King David, "God has blessed Obededom's house and everything he has because of the ark of God." So David went and happily moved the ark of God from Obededom's house to the city of David.
2 Samuel 6:13 When those carrying the ark of God had walked six steps, he offered oxen and fattened animals as sacrifices.
2 Samuel 6:14 David danced before God with all his strength, wearing a linen garment.
2 Samuel 6:15 So David and all of Israel's family moved the ark of God with loud cheers and trumpet blasts.
2 Samuel 6:16 As God's ark entered David's city, Saul's daughter Michal saw King David jumping and dancing before God through a window and she felt contempt for him inside.
2 Samuel 6:17 They brought God's ark and put it where it should be, in the tent David set up for it. David made burnt offerings and peace offerings to God.
2 Samuel 6:18 After David finished offering burnt and peace offerings, he blessed the people in God's name.
2 Samuel 6:19 He gave out to everyone there, both women and men, a loaf of bread, a good serving of meat, and a bottle of wine. Then all the people went home.
2 Samuel 6:20 David went back to bless his family. Michal, Saul's daughter, met David and said, "The king of Israel looked foolish today, exposing himself in front of the servant girls like a shameless man!"
2 Samuel 6:21 David said to Michal, "I did it for God, who picked me instead of your dad and his family to be the leader of God's people, Israel. That's why I will celebrate before God."
2 Samuel 6:22 I will be even more undignified than this, and I will be humble in my own eyes. But by the female servants you mentioned, I will be respected.
2 Samuel 6:23 So Michal, Saul's daughter, had no children until she died.

2 Samuel 7:1 When the king was in his house, and God had given him peace from all his enemies;
2 Samuel 7:2 The king said to the prophet Nathan, "Look, I live in a cedar house, but God's ark stays in a tent."
2 Samuel 7:3 Nathan told the king, "Go ahead and do everything you want to do because God is with you."
2 Samuel 7:4 That night, God's message came to Nathan, saying,
2 Samuel 7:5 Go and tell my servant David, God says, Will you build me a house to live in?
2 Samuel 7:6 Since I led the people of Israel out of Egypt, I have never lived in a house. Instead, I have moved in a tent and in a shelter.
2 Samuel 7:7 In every place where I have been with all of Israel's children, did I ever ask any tribe I told to take care of my people Israel, "Why don't you build me a cedar house?"
2 Samuel 7:8 So now, tell my servant David this: God says, 'I chose you from the pasture and from tending the sheep to be the leader of my people, Israel.'
2 Samuel 7:9 I was with you wherever you went, and I defeated all your enemies, making your name as great as the most famous people on earth.
2 Samuel 7:10 I will provide a home for my people Israel and settle them so they can live in their own place without moving again; evil people will not trouble them anymore, like in the past.
2 Samuel 7:11 Ever since I appointed leaders for my people Israel and gave you peace from all your enemies, God has promised to build you a house.
2 Samuel 7:12 When your time comes to an end and you die, I will raise up your descendants to follow you, one who will come from your own body, and I will make his kingdom strong.
2 Samuel 7:13 He will build a house for my name, and I will establish his kingdom's throne forever.
2 Samuel 7:14 I will be his father, and he will be my son. If he does wrong, I will correct him with punishment from people and their whippings.
2 Samuel 7:15 My kindness will not leave him, as I took it from Saul, whom I removed before you.
2 Samuel 7:16 Your family and kingdom will last forever; your rule will go on forever.
2 Samuel 7:17 Nathan told David everything he had heard and seen.
2 Samuel 7:18 Then King David went in, sat before God, and said, "Who am I, God, and what is my family, that you have brought me this far?"
2 Samuel 7:19 This was still a small thing to you, God, but you also promised good things for your servant's family far into the future. Is this how people normally act, God?
2 Samuel 7:20 What more can David say to you? You, God, know your servant.
2 Samuel 7:21 For the sake of your promise and your own desire, you have done all these amazing things so that your servant could understand them.
2 Samuel 7:22 You are great, God, because there is no one like you, and there is no other God, just as we have heard.
2 Samuel 7:23 What other nation on earth is like your people Israel? God chose them to be his own, to make himself known, and to perform great and awe-inspiring acts for them—clearing out nations and their gods to free Israel from Egypt.
2 Samuel 7:24 You have made the people of Israel your own people forever, and you, God, have become their God.
2 Samuel 7:25 Now, God, make true your promise about your servant and his family forever, and do as you have promised.
2 Samuel 7:26 May your name be honored always, as people say, "God rules over Israel," and may David's family remain strong in your presence.
2 Samuel 7:27 You, God of all and God of Israel, have told your servant that you will build a house for him. So your servant has decided to pray this prayer to you.
2 Samuel 7:28 And now, God, you are that God, your words are true, and you have promised this goodness to your servant.
2 Samuel 7:29 Please bless your servant's house so it can last forever in your presence. You, God, have promised this; may your blessing make your servant's house forever blessed.

2 Samuel 8:1 After this, David defeated the Philistines and brought them under control; David also captured Methegammah from the Philistines.
2 Samuel 8:2 He defeated the Moabites and used a rope to measure them, laying them on the ground. Those measured by two lengths of rope were killed, and those by one length were spared. Thus, the Moabites served David and brought him presents.
2 Samuel 8:3 David struck Hadadezer, Rehob's son and king of Zobah, while he was trying to take back his territory at the Euphrates River.
2 Samuel 8:4 David captured from him a thousand chariots, seven hundred horsemen, and twenty thousand soldiers. David crippled all the chariot horses, but saved enough for one hundred chariots.
2 Samuel 8:5 When the Syrians from Damascus helped Hadadezer, the king of Zobah, David killed twenty-two thousand Syrian men.
2 Samuel 8:6 David placed military camps in Damascus, Syria, and the Syrians worked for David and gave him presents. God protected David everywhere he went.
2 Samuel 8:7 David took the gold shields from Hadadezer's servants and brought them to Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 8:8 From Betah and Berothai, towns of Hadadezer, King David captured a lot of bronze.
2 Samuel 8:9 When Toi, the king of Hamath, learned that David had defeated the entire army of Hadadezer,
2 Samuel 8:10 Then Toi sent his son Joram to King David to greet him and bless him because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him; Hadadezer had been at war with Toi. Joram brought with him silver, gold, and bronze items.
2 Samuel 8:11 King David also set apart for God the silver and gold he had dedicated from all the nations he conquered.
2 Samuel 8:12 From Syria, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and the loot from Hadadezer, son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
2 Samuel 8:13 David became famous when he returned from defeating the Syrians in the Salt Valley, where he had killed eighteen thousand men.
2 Samuel 8:14 He placed guards in Edom; he put guards all over Edom, and everyone in Edom served David. God protected David wherever he went.
2 Samuel 8:15 David ruled over all Israel and he gave fair decisions and justice to all his people.
2 Samuel 8:16 Joab, son of Zeruiah, was in command of the army, and Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, was the record keeper.
2 Samuel 8:17 Zadok, Ahitub's son, and Ahimelech, Abiathar's son, were priests; Seraiah was the secretary.
2 Samuel 8:18 Benaiah, Jehoiada's son, led both the Cherethites and Pelethites; David's sons were the main leaders.

2 Samuel 9:1 David asked, "Is there anyone still alive from Saul's family, so I can be kind to them for Jonathan's sake?"
2 Samuel 9:2 Saul's household had a servant named Ziba. When they brought him to David, the king asked, "Are you Ziba?" He replied, "I am your servant."
2 Samuel 9:3 The king asked, "Is there no one left from Saul's family to whom I can show God's kindness?" Ziba told the king, "Jonathan has a son who cannot walk."
2 Samuel 9:4 The king asked him, "Where is he?" Ziba answered the king, "Look, he's at the house of Machir, Ammiel's son, in Lodebar."
2 Samuel 9:5 Then King David sent for him and brought him from Machir's house, the son of Ammiel, in Lodebar.
2 Samuel 9:6 When Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son and Saul's grandson, came to David, he bowed down to show respect. David called out, "Mephibosheth!" And he replied, "Here I am, your servant!"
2 Samuel 9:7 David told him, "Don't be afraid. I will definitely be kind to you because of your father Jonathan. I will give back to you all the land of your grandfather Saul, and you will always eat at my table."
2 Samuel 9:8 He bowed and said, "What is your servant, that you would notice a worthless dog like me?"
2 Samuel 9:9 The king called Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, "I have given your master's son everything that belonged to Saul and his family."
2 Samuel 9:10 You, your sons, and your workers must farm the land for him, and you must bring in the crops so that your master's son will have food to eat; but Mephibosheth, your master's son, will always eat bread at my table. Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty workers.
2 Samuel 9:11 Ziba told the king, "I will do everything you, the king, have told me to do." The king said about Mephibosheth, "He will eat at my table like one of my sons."
2 Samuel 9:12 Mephibosheth had a young son named Micha. Everyone living in Ziba's house served Mephibosheth.
2 Samuel 9:13 Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem because he always ate at the king's table, and he could not walk well with either of his feet.

2 Samuel 10:1 After this, the king of Ammon died, and his son Hanun became king in his place.
2 Samuel 10:2 David said, "I will be kind to Hanun, Nahash's son, just as his father was kind to me." David sent his servants to comfort Hanun because of his father's death. David's servants entered the land of the Ammonites.
2 Samuel 10:3 The leaders of the Ammonites said to their king Hanun, "Do you think David is honoring your father by sending these men to comfort you? Hasn't David actually sent them to explore the city, spy on it, and destroy it?"
2 Samuel 10:4 So Hanun took David's servants, shaved half of their beards, cut their clothes up to their bottoms, and sent them away.
2 Samuel 10:5 When they shared this with David, he went out to meet them because the men felt very ashamed. The king said, "Stay at Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then come back."
2 Samuel 10:6 When the Ammonites realized that David disliked them, they hired twenty thousand Syrian soldiers from Bethrehob and Zoba, a thousand from King Maacah, and twelve thousand from Ishtob.
2 Samuel 10:7 When David found out, he sent Joab and all his strong soldiers.
2 Samuel 10:8 The Ammonites came and prepared for battle at the gate entrance, while the Syrians from Zoba, Rehob, Ishtob, and Maacah stood alone in the field.
2 Samuel 10:9 When Joab realized he was surrounded by the enemy in front and behind, he picked the best soldiers of Israel and arranged them to fight the Syrians.
2 Samuel 10:10 He gave the rest of the people to his brother Abishai to arrange them for battle against the Ammonites.
2 Samuel 10:11 He said, "If the Syrians are too powerful for me, then you must help me. But if the Ammonites are too powerful for you, I will come and help you."
2 Samuel 10:12 Be brave, let's fight for our people and God's cities, and let God do what he thinks is best.
2 Samuel 10:13 Joab and his soldiers moved closer to fight the Syrians, and the Syrians ran away from them.
2 Samuel 10:14 When the Ammonites saw that the Syrians had run away, they also ran from Abishai and went back to their city. Then Joab left the Ammonites and went to Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 10:15 When the Syrians realized they were defeated by Israel, they joined forces.
2 Samuel 10:16 Hadarezer called and gathered the Syrians from across the river, and they went to Helam with their leader Shobach marching in front.
2 Samuel 10:17 When David heard the news, he brought all of Israel together, crossed the Jordan River, and went to Helam. The Syrians lined up to fight against David and battled with him.
2 Samuel 10:18 The Syrians ran away from Israel; David killed 700 of their chariot men, 40,000 on horseback, and struck their leader Shobach, who died there.
2 Samuel 10:19 When all the kings who served Hadarezer saw they were defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and worked for them. So, the Syrians were afraid to help the people of Ammon again.

2 Samuel 11:1 After a year ended, when kings usually went to war, David sent Joab, his officers, and all Israel. They defeated the Ammonites and surrounded Rabbah. But David stayed in Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 11:2 One evening, David got up from his bed, walked on the palace roof, and saw a very beautiful woman bathing.
2 Samuel 11:3 David sent someone to find out about the woman. Someone asked, "Isn't this Bathsheba, Eliam's daughter, Uriah the Hittite's wife?"
2 Samuel 11:4 David sent people to get her. She came to him, and they slept together after she was clean from her impurity. Then she went back home.
2 Samuel 11:5 The woman became pregnant, and she sent word to David, saying, "I am expecting a baby."
2 Samuel 11:6 David sent a message to Joab: "Send me Uriah the Hittite." So Joab sent Uriah to David.
2 Samuel 11:7 When Uriah came to him, David asked how Joab was, how the people were, and how the war was going.
2 Samuel 11:8 David told Uriah, "Go to your house and wash your feet." Uriah left the king's house, and a serving of food from the king was sent after him.
2 Samuel 11:9 Uriah slept at the entrance of the king's house with all his master's servants and did not go down to his own home.
2 Samuel 11:10 When they told David, "Uriah did not go home," David asked Uriah, "Didn't you come from a trip? Why didn't you go home?"
2 Samuel 11:11 Uriah said to David, "The ark, and Israel, and Judah stay in tents; and my leader Joab, and my lord's servants, camp in the fields. Should I then go to my house to eat, drink, and be with my wife? As you live, and as your spirit lives, I will not do this."
2 Samuel 11:12 David told Uriah, "Stay here today as well, and tomorrow I will let you go." So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next day.
2 Samuel 11:13 When David invited him, he ate and drank in front of David, and David got him drunk. In the evening, he went to sleep on his bed with his master's servants instead of going home.
2 Samuel 11:14 In the morning, David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it with Uriah.
2 Samuel 11:15 He wrote in the letter: Place Uriah at the front where the fighting is fiercest and then pull back so he will be struck down and die.
2 Samuel 11:16 When Joab saw the city, he sent Uriah to a place where he knew strong soldiers were.
2 Samuel 11:17 The city men came out, fought with Joab, and some of David's servants died, including Uriah the Hittite.
2 Samuel 11:18 Then Joab sent a message to tell David everything about the war.
2 Samuel 11:19 He gave the messenger instructions, saying, "After you finish reporting the war news to the king,
2 Samuel 11:20 If the king gets angry and asks you why you came so close to the city during the battle, didn't you realize they would shoot arrows from the wall?
2 Samuel 11:21 Who killed Abimelech, son of Jerubbesheth? Wasn't it a woman who dropped a millstone on him from the wall so he died in Thebez? Why did you go close to the wall? Then you must say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead.'
2 Samuel 11:22 The messenger went, came, and told David everything Joab had sent him to say.
2 Samuel 11:23 The messenger told David, "The men were too strong for us. They attacked us in the open field, but we fought them off all the way to the city gate."
2 Samuel 11:24 The archers shot arrows at your servants from the wall; some of the king's servants have died, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead.
2 Samuel 11:25 David told the messenger, "Tell Joab, 'Don't be upset about this because the sword takes one as well as another. Fight harder against the city, destroy it, and cheer him up.'"
2 Samuel 11:26 When Uriah's wife learned that her husband Uriah had died, she grieved for him.
2 Samuel 11:27 After the mourning ended, David brought her to his house, she became his wife, and had a son for him. But what David did made God unhappy.

2 Samuel 12:1 God sent Nathan to David. He went to him and said, "There were two men in the same city; one was rich and the other was poor."
2 Samuel 12:2 The rich man had very many sheep and cattle.
2 Samuel 12:3 The poor man had only one small female lamb he had bought and cared for. It grew up with him and his children, eating from his food, drinking from his cup, and sleeping close to him, like a daughter to him.
2 Samuel 12:4 A traveler came to the rich man, but he didn't want to use any of his own sheep or cattle to cook for the guest. Instead, he took the poor man's only lamb and prepared it for his visitor.
2 Samuel 12:5 David became very angry at the man and said to Nathan, "As God lives, this man who did this must die."
2 Samuel 12:6 He must return four sheep for the one he took because he did this and had no mercy.
2 Samuel 12:7 Nathan told David, "You are the man. God says, I made you king over Israel, and I saved you from Saul's power."
2 Samuel 12:8 I gave you your master's house and his wives, and the kingdoms of Israel and Judah; if that wasn't enough, I would have given you even more.
2 Samuel 12:9 Why have you ignored God's command by doing wrong in his eyes? You killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword, took his wife as your own, and killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.
2 Samuel 12:10 So now, the sword will always be in your family because you looked down on me and took Uriah the Hittite's wife to be your own.
2 Samuel 12:11 God says, "Look, I will bring trouble on you from your own family. I will take your wives while you watch and give them to your neighbor. He will sleep with your wives in broad daylight."
2 Samuel 12:12 You did it in secret, but I will do this for all Israel to see, under the sun.
2 Samuel 12:13 David told Nathan, "I have sinned against God." Nathan replied to David, "God has forgiven your sin; you will not die."
2 Samuel 12:14 However, because this action of yours has given God's enemies a big reason to insult, the baby born to you will certainly die.
2 Samuel 12:15 Nathan went to his home. God made the child that Uriah's wife had with David very ill.
2 Samuel 12:16 David prayed to God for the child; David fasted, went inside, and spent the whole night lying on the ground.
2 Samuel 12:17 The older leaders of his house stood up and went to him to help him get up from the ground, but he refused, and he did not eat bread with them.
2 Samuel 12:18 On the seventh day, the child died. David's servants were afraid to tell him the child was dead. They thought, "When the child was still alive, we spoke to him, and he didn't listen to us. How upset will he be if we tell him the child is dead?"
2 Samuel 12:19 When David noticed his servants whispering, he realized the child had died. So David asked them, "Is the child dead?" They replied, "Yes, he is dead."
2 Samuel 12:20 David got up from the ground, washed, put on lotion, changed his clothes, went to God's house, and prayed. Then he went home, and when he asked for food, they gave him some, and he ate.
2 Samuel 12:21 His servants asked him, "Why have you done this? You fasted and cried for the child when it was alive; but after the child died, you got up and ate."
2 Samuel 12:22 He said, "When the child was still alive, I fasted and cried because I thought, 'Maybe God will be kind to me so the child will live.'"
2 Samuel 12:23 He is dead now. Why should I fast? Can I make him live again? I will go to him, but he will not come back to me.
2 Samuel 12:24 David comforted his wife Bathsheba, and slept with her. She had a son, and David named him Solomon. God loved him.
2 Samuel 12:25 He sent the prophet Nathan to name him Jedidiah because of God.
2 Samuel 12:26 Joab battled Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the main city.
2 Samuel 12:27 Joab sent people to tell David, "I have battled Rabbah and captured the water city."
2 Samuel 12:28 Now get the rest of the people, camp around the city, and capture it, so I don't take the city and have it named after me.
2 Samuel 12:29 David brought all the people, went to Rabbah, fought against it, and captured it.
2 Samuel 12:30 He took the crown from their king's head. It weighed a talent of gold and had precious stones. It was placed on David's head. He took a lot of valuable things from the city.
2 Samuel 12:31 He took the people out of the city, made them work with saws, iron tools, and axes, and had them make bricks. David did this to all the Ammonite cities, then he and his people went back to Jerusalem.

2 Samuel 13:1 After this, David's son Absalom had a beautiful sister named Tamar, and David's son Amnon loved her.
2 Samuel 13:2 Amnon was so upset that he became sick because of his sister Tamar; she was a virgin, and Amnon found it difficult to do anything to her.
2 Samuel 13:3 Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, who was the son of Shimeah, David's brother, and Jonadab was very clever.
2 Samuel 13:4 He asked him, "Why are you, the king's son, getting thinner every day? Won't you tell me?" Amnon replied, "I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister."
2 Samuel 13:5 Jonadab told him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be sick. When your father comes to see you, ask him, 'Please let my sister Tamar come and give me food. Let her prepare the food in front of me so I can watch and eat from her hand.'"
2 Samuel 13:6 Amnon laid down and pretended to be sick. When the king came to visit him, Amnon asked the king, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make some cakes where I can see her, so I can eat from her hand."
2 Samuel 13:7 David sent a message to Tamar, saying, "Go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him."
2 Samuel 13:8 Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house where he was lying down. She mixed flour, shaped it, and cooked cakes where he could see her.
2 Samuel 13:9 She got a pan and put the food in front of him, but he wouldn't eat. Amnon said, "Send everyone away from me." So everyone left him.
2 Samuel 13:10 Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food to the room so I can eat from your hand." Tamar took the cakes she made and brought them to the room for her brother Amnon.
2 Samuel 13:11 When she brought him the food, he grabbed her and said, "Come sleep with me, my sister."
2 Samuel 13:12 She replied, "No, my brother, don't force me. Such things should not happen in Israel. Don't do this foolish act."
2 Samuel 13:13 Where can I hide my shame? And you will be like a fool in Israel. So please, ask the king; he won't keep me from you.
2 Samuel 13:14 However, he refused to listen to her and, being stronger than her, overpowered her and slept with her.
2 Samuel 13:15 Then Amnon hated her very much; the hate he felt for her was stronger than his previous love. Amnon said to her, "Get up and leave."
2 Samuel 13:16 She told him, "No reason for this; sending me away is worse than what you did before." But he didn't listen to her.
2 Samuel 13:17 He called his servant who worked for him and said, "Now take this woman out of here and lock the door behind her."
2 Samuel 13:18 She wore a robe of many colors because that's what unmarried princesses wore. Afterward, his servant took her out and locked the door behind her.
2 Samuel 13:19 Tamar put ash on her head, tore her colorful robe, placed her hand on her head, and walked away crying.
2 Samuel 13:20 Absalom, her brother, asked her, "Did Amnon, your brother, hurt you? Stay quiet now, my sister; he's your brother. Don't worry about this." So Tamar stayed alone in her brother Absalom's home.
2 Samuel 13:21 When King David heard about all this, he was very angry.
2 Samuel 13:22 Absalom said nothing, good or bad, to his brother Amnon because Absalom hated Amnon for hurting their sister Tamar.
2 Samuel 13:23 Two years later, Absalom held a sheep shearing event in Baalhazor, near Ephraim, and he invited all the king's sons.
2 Samuel 13:24 Absalom went to the king and said, "Look, I have people who are shearing sheep. Please let the king and his servants join me."
2 Samuel 13:25 The king told Absalom, "No, my son, we should not all go now, so we don't become a burden to you." Even though he urged him, he did not go, but gave him his blessing.
2 Samuel 13:26 Then Absalom said, "If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us." And the king asked, "Why should he go with you?"
2 Samuel 13:27 But Absalom insisted until he convinced Amnon and all the king's sons to go with him.
2 Samuel 13:28 Absalom told his servants, "Watch when Amnon gets happy from drinking wine, and when I tell you to hit Amnon, then kill him. Don't be afraid; haven't I given you orders? Be brave and strong."
2 Samuel 13:29 Absalom's servants did to Amnon what Absalom ordered. Then all the king's sons got up, each one mounted his mule, and they all ran away.
2 Samuel 13:30 While they were traveling, news reached David that Absalom had killed all the king's sons and not one of them had survived.
2 Samuel 13:31 Then the king got up, tore his clothes, and lay on the ground; all his servants stood nearby with their clothes torn.
2 Samuel 13:32 Jonadab, Shimeah's son and David's nephew, said, "My lord should not think that all the young princes have been killed. Only Amnon is dead. This was planned by Absalom since the day he hurt his sister Tamar."
2 Samuel 13:33 So now, let the king not worry, thinking all his sons are dead. Only Amnon is dead.
2 Samuel 13:34 Absalom ran away. The young man on guard looked up and saw many people coming from the hillside behind him.
2 Samuel 13:35 Jonadab told the king, "Look, the king's sons are coming; it's just as your servant said."
2 Samuel 13:36 After he finished speaking, the king's sons arrived, cried loudly, and wept, and the king and all his servants also wept bitterly.
2 Samuel 13:37 Absalom ran away and went to Talmai, son of Ammihud, the king of Geshur. David grieved for his son every day.
2 Samuel 13:38 Absalom ran away to Geshur and stayed there for three years.
2 Samuel 13:39 King David deeply wanted to see Absalom because he felt better about Amnon now that he was dead.

2 Samuel 14:1 Joab, Zeruiah's son, noticed that the king felt kindly toward Absalom.
2 Samuel 14:2 Joab sent to Tekoah and brought back a smart woman and said to her, "Please pretend to be grieving. Dress in sad clothes and don't put on any perfume. Act like you have been mourning a death for a long time."
2 Samuel 14:3 Go to the king and say these things to him. So Joab gave her the words to say.
2 Samuel 14:4 When the woman from Tekoah spoke to the king, she bowed down with her face to the ground and said, "Help me, O king."
2 Samuel 14:5 The king asked her, "What's wrong?" She answered, "I am truly a widow; my husband has died."
2 Samuel 14:6 Your servant had two sons, and they fought in the field with no one to separate them, and one hit the other and killed him.
2 Samuel 14:7 Look, the whole family has turned against your servant, and they said, 'Hand over the one who hit his brother, so we can kill him for taking his brother's life; and we want to get rid of the heir too. This way, they would put out the only surviving part of my family, leaving my husband with no one to carry on his name or future on earth.
2 Samuel 14:8 The king told the woman, "Go to your home, and I will take care of you."
2 Samuel 14:9 The woman from Tekoah said to the king, "My king, let the wrong be my fault and my family's fault, and let the king and his throne be innocent."
2 Samuel 14:10 And the king said, "If anyone bothers you, bring them to me, and they won't bother you again."
2 Samuel 14:11 She said, "Please, let the king remember God, so you don't let those seeking revenge kill again, or they might kill my son." He replied, "As long as God lives, not a single hair from your son's head will fall to the ground."
2 Samuel 14:12 Then the woman said, "Please let me, your servant, say one thing to you, the king." And he replied, "Go ahead."
2 Samuel 14:13 The woman asked, "Why have you planned something so harmful against God's people? The king talks like he's wrong because he doesn't bring back his exiled ones."
2 Samuel 14:14 We must die and are like water poured on the ground that can't be collected again; God doesn't favor anyone, yet he finds ways to keep his exiled people close to him.
2 Samuel 14:15 So now I have come to talk to the king about this matter because the people made me scared: and I thought, 'I will speak to the king; perhaps the king will do what I ask.'
2 Samuel 14:16 The king will listen and save his servant from the man who wants to kill me and my son, taking away God's inheritance from us.
2 Samuel 14:17 Then I thought, 'My king's decision will bring peace.' You have the wisdom of an angel from God to know right from wrong, so God will be with you.
2 Samuel 14:18 The king replied to the woman, "Please don't hide what I'm about to ask you." The woman said, "Go ahead, your majesty, ask me."
2 Samuel 14:19 The king asked, "Isn't Joab involved in all this with you?" The woman replied, "I swear by your life, my king, no one can ignore any of your words. Your servant Joab told me what to do and said exactly what I should say."
2 Samuel 14:20 Joab did this to make this conversation happen, and my master is as wise as an angel of God, knowing everything on earth.
2 Samuel 14:21 The king told Joab, "Look, I have decided: go and bring back the young man Absalom."
2 Samuel 14:22 Joab fell to the ground, facedown, and bowed, thanking the king. Joab said, "Today, I, your servant, know that I am favored by you, my lord, the king, because you have granted your servant's request."
2 Samuel 14:23 Joab got up, went to Geshur, and brought Absalom back to Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 14:24 The king said, "Let him go to his own house and not see me." So Absalom went to his house and did not see the king.
2 Samuel 14:25 But in all Israel, no one was as praised for their beauty as Absalom; from his foot to his head, he had no flaws.
2 Samuel 14:26 Every year, he cut his hair because it was too heavy. When he cut it, he found it weighed two hundred shekels by the royal standard.
2 Samuel 14:27 Absalom had three sons and one daughter named Tamar; she was very beautiful.
2 Samuel 14:28 Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years without seeing the king.
2 Samuel 14:29 So Absalom asked Joab to bring him to the king, but Joab refused to come. Even when Absalom asked a second time, Joab wouldn't come.
2 Samuel 14:30 So he told his servants, "Look, Joab's field is next to mine and it has barley; go and burn it." Then Absalom's servants burned the field.
2 Samuel 14:31 Joab got up, went to Absalom's house, and asked him, "Why did your servants burn my field?"
2 Samuel 14:32 Absalom said to Joab, "Look, I called for you, telling you to come here so I could send you to the king and ask, 'Why did I leave Geshur? It would have been better for me to stay there. Now let me see the king, and if I have done wrong, let him put me to death.'"
2 Samuel 14:33 Joab went to the king and told him. When Absalom was called, he went to the king, bowed with his face to the ground, and the king kissed Absalom.

2 Samuel 15:1 After this, Absalom got chariots, horses, and fifty men to run ahead of him.
2 Samuel 15:2 Absalom got up early and stood by the gate's path. Whenever someone with a problem came to the king for a decision, Absalom would call them over and ask, "Which city are you from?" And the person would answer, "I am from one of Israel's tribes."
2 Samuel 15:3 Absalom told him, "Look, your issues are fair and correct; but there's no one appointed by the king to listen to you."
2 Samuel 15:4 Absalom also said, "I wish I were the judge of the land, so everyone with any issue could come to me, and I would give them fairness!"
2 Samuel 15:5 Whenever someone came close to honor him, he reached out his hand, grabbed them, and kissed them.
2 Samuel 15:6 Absalom acted this way toward all Israelites who came to the king for a decision: so Absalom won over the hearts of the people of Israel.
2 Samuel 15:7 After forty years, Absalom asked the king, "Please let me go to Hebron to keep my promise to God."
2 Samuel 15:8 I made a promise when I was staying in Geshur, in Syria. I said, "If God brings me back to Jerusalem, I will serve God."
2 Samuel 15:9 The king told him, "Leave in peace." So he got up and went to Hebron.
2 Samuel 15:10 Absalom sent spies to all of Israel's tribes, telling them, "When you hear the trumpet, say 'Absalom is king in Hebron.'"
2 Samuel 15:11 Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom because they were invited. They went innocently, not knowing anything.
2 Samuel 15:12 Absalom called for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's advisor, from his city Giloh while he was making sacrifices. The plot grew powerful because more and more people joined Absalom.
2 Samuel 15:13 A messenger came to David and said, "The people of Israel are following Absalom."
2 Samuel 15:14 David told his servants in Jerusalem, "Get up and let's run away. We can't escape from Absalom if we don't. Hurry and leave, or he will catch us quickly, hurt us, and attack the city with his sword."
2 Samuel 15:15 The king's helpers told the king, "Look, we are your helpers, ready to do whatever the king decides."
2 Samuel 15:16 The king went out, and his whole family followed. He left ten women concubines to take care of the house.
2 Samuel 15:17 The king set out, and everyone followed him, and they stopped at a place that was far away.
2 Samuel 15:18 All his helpers walked past him; the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and the Gittites, six hundred men who followed him from Gath, walked ahead of the king.
2 Samuel 15:19 The king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why are you also coming with us? Go back to your home and stay with the king: you are a foreigner and an exile."
2 Samuel 15:20 Since you only arrived yesterday, should I make you move around with us today? I will go wherever I can, so go back and take your brothers with you. May mercy and truth be with you.
2 Samuel 15:21 Ittai told the king, "As God is alive, and as you, the king, are alive, I promise wherever you are, whether dead or alive, I will be there too."
2 Samuel 15:22 David said to Ittai, "Go and cross over." Ittai the Gittite and all his men and the children with him crossed over.
2 Samuel 15:23 Everyone in the land cried loudly, and all the people crossed the river. The king crossed the Kidron stream too, and all the people went toward the desert way.
2 Samuel 15:24 Look, Zadok and all the Levites were with him, carrying God's covenant box. They put down God's box, and Abiathar left when all the people finished leaving the city.
2 Samuel 15:25 The king told Zadok, "Take the ark of God back to the city. If God is pleased with me, he will let me come back to see it and his dwelling place again."
2 Samuel 15:26 But if he says, "I don't enjoy you"; look, I am here, let him do to me what seems good to him.
2 Samuel 15:27 The king told Zadok the priest, "Aren't you a prophet? Go back to the city in peace, with your two sons, Ahimaaz your son, and Jonathan, Abiathar's son."
2 Samuel 15:28 Look, I will wait in the desert plain until you send me a message to inform me.
2 Samuel 15:29 So Zadok and Abiathar took the ark of God back to Jerusalem and stayed there.
2 Samuel 15:30 David climbed the slope of the Mount of Olives, crying as he climbed, with his head covered and barefoot. Everyone with him also covered their heads, all crying while going up.
2 Samuel 15:31 Someone told David, "Ahithophel is working with Absalom against you." And David prayed, "God, please make Ahithophel's advice seem foolish."
2 Samuel 15:32 When David reached the mountaintop where he worshipped God, Hushai the Archite approached him with his coat torn and dirt on his head.
2 Samuel 15:33 David said, "If you come with me, then you will be a burden to me."
2 Samuel 15:34 If you go back to the city and tell Absalom, "I will serve you, king, like I served your father before," then you can help stop Ahithophel's plan for me.
2 Samuel 15:35 Don't you have Zadok and Abiathar, the priests, with you? So, whatever you hear from the king's house, tell it to Zadok and Abiathar, the priests.
2 Samuel 15:36 Look, they have their two sons with them there, Ahimaaz, Zadok's son, and Jonathan, Abiathar's son. Use them to send me any news you hear.
2 Samuel 15:37 Hushai, David's friend, entered the city while Absalom entered Jerusalem.

2 Samuel 16:1 When David had just gone over the hilltop, Ziba, who worked for Mephibosheth, came to meet him. He had two saddled donkeys with him, as well as two hundred loaves of bread, one hundred bunches of raisins, one hundred summer fruits, and a bottle of wine.
2 Samuel 16:2 The king asked Ziba, "What are these for?" Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's family to ride; the bread and summer fruit are for the young men to eat; and the wine is for anyone who is weak in the desert to drink."
2 Samuel 16:3 The king asked, "Where is your master's son?" Ziba told the king, "He is staying in Jerusalem, because he believes that today, Israel will give him back my father's kingdom."
2 Samuel 16:4 Then the king told Ziba, "Look, everything that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." And Ziba replied, "I hope to find favor in your eyes, my lord, O king."
2 Samuel 16:5 When King David reached Bahurim, a man from Saul's family named Shimei, the son of Gera, came out. He kept cursing as he approached.
2 Samuel 16:6 He threw stones at David and all of King David's servants; all the people and brave warriors were to his right and left.
2 Samuel 16:7 Shimei cursed, saying, "Get out, get out, you murderer, you worthless man!"
2 Samuel 16:8 God has brought back all the bloodshed of Saul's family, which you ruled after, onto you; and God has given your kingdom to Absalom, your son. Now you are caught because of your violence, for you are a man of bloodshed.
2 Samuel 16:9 Abishai, Zeruiah's son, said to the king, "Why should this worthless man insult my king? Please let me go and cut off his head."
2 Samuel 16:10 The king asked, "Why should I bother with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse me if God told him to curse David. Who can question why he does it?"
2 Samuel 16:11 David said to Abishai and all his servants, "Look, my own son wants to kill me. So even more, this man from Benjamin might do it. Let him be and let him curse, because God has told him to."
2 Samuel 16:12 Maybe God will see my suffering and reward me with good for being cursed today.
2 Samuel 16:13 As David and his men traveled, Shimei walked on the hillside opposite them, cursed them as he moved, threw stones, and scattered dust at them.
2 Samuel 16:14 The king and everyone with him arrived tired and rested there.
2 Samuel 16:15 Absalom and all the Israelite men came to Jerusalem with Ahithophel.
2 Samuel 16:16 When Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, "May God protect the king, may God protect the king."
2 Samuel 16:17 Absalom asked Hushai, "Is this how you show loyalty to your friend? Why didn't you go with your friend?"
2 Samuel 16:18 Hushai told Absalom, "No; I will serve the one God and the people of Israel choose, and I will stay with him."
2 Samuel 16:19 Again, who should I serve? Shouldn't I serve before his son? Just as I served before your father, I will serve before you.
2 Samuel 16:20 Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Tell us what we should do."
2 Samuel 16:21 Ahithophel told Absalom to sleep with his father's concubines, who were left to take care of the house. Then everyone in Israel will know that his father is against him, which will make everyone supporting him feel stronger.
2 Samuel 16:22 They set up a tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom slept with his father's women for all Israel to see.
2 Samuel 16:23 Ahithophel's advice back then was so good, it was like asking God directly. Both David and Absalom valued all of Ahithophel's advice.

2 Samuel 17:1 Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Let me pick twelve thousand men and go after David tonight."
2 Samuel 17:2 I will attack him when he is tired and his hands are weak, making him scared. Everyone with him will run away, and I will strike down only the king.
2 Samuel 17:3 I will return all the people to you: it's like everyone has come back because you're looking for one man: this way, everyone will be at peace.
2 Samuel 17:4 Absalom and all the leaders of Israel liked the idea.
2 Samuel 17:5 Then Absalom said, "Call Hushai the Archite too, so we can hear what he has to say."
2 Samuel 17:6 When Hushai arrived, Absalom asked him, "Ahithophel has given this advice. Should we follow it? If not, you tell us what to do."
2 Samuel 17:7 Hushai told Absalom, "The advice Ahithophel has given is not good right now."
2 Samuel 17:8 Hushai said, you know your father and his men are strong, and they are upset like a bear whose cubs are taken in the field; your father is a warrior and won't stay with the people.
2 Samuel 17:9 Look, he's hiding in a pit or another place. And if some of his men fall at first, anyone who hears will say, 'There's a killing among Absalom's followers.'
2 Samuel 17:10 Even the brave person, with a heart like a lion's, will be completely afraid because everyone in Israel knows your father is a strong man, and those with him are courageous.
2 Samuel 17:11 So I suggest you bring together all of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, like the countless grains of sand by the sea; and you yourself should go into the battle.
2 Samuel 17:12 We will find him in some place, and we will surprise him like dew falls on the ground: not one of him or his men will remain.
2 Samuel 17:13 Furthermore, if he enters a city, then all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we will pull it into the river until not even one small stone is left there.
2 Samuel 17:14 Absalom and all the Israelite men said, "Hushai the Archite's advice is better than Ahithophel's advice." This happened because God planned to ruin Ahithophel's good advice, so that He could bring disaster on Absalom.
2 Samuel 17:15 Hushai said to Zadok and Abiathar, the priests, "Ahithophel gave this advice to Absalom and Israel's leaders, and I gave this advice."
2 Samuel 17:16 So now, send a message to David fast. Say to him, "Don't stay tonight in the desert fields, but hurry and cross the river, so that the king and everyone with him aren't caught."
2 Samuel 17:17 Jonathan and Ahimaaz stayed at Enrogel because they didn't want to be seen entering the city. A young woman went to tell them, and they went to inform King David.
2 Samuel 17:18 However, a boy saw them and informed Absalom. They both hurried away and reached a man's house in Bahurim, with a well in his yard, which they entered.
2 Samuel 17:19 The woman covered the well's opening with a cloth and scattered crushed grain on it; and no one knew about it.
2 Samuel 17:20 When Absalom's servants went to the woman's house, they asked, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" The woman told them, "They crossed the water stream." After searching and not finding them, the servants went back to Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 17:21 After they left, they climbed out of the well, went to tell King David, and said, "Get up and cross the river quickly, because Ahithophel has advised this against you."
2 Samuel 17:22 Then David got up, and everyone with him crossed the Jordan River. By dawn, every one of them had crossed over.
2 Samuel 17:23 When Ahithophel realized his advice was ignored, he prepared his donkey, left, went to his home in his city, arranged his affairs, hanged himself, died, and was buried in his father's tomb.
2 Samuel 17:24 David arrived at Mahanaim. Absalom crossed the Jordan River with all the men of Israel.
2 Samuel 17:25 Absalom appointed Amasa as the army's leader in place of Joab. Amasa's father was Ithra, an Israelite, who had been with Abigail, daughter of Nahash and sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.
2 Samuel 17:26 Israel and Absalom set up camp in the land of Gilead.
2 Samuel 17:27 When David got to Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim.
2 Samuel 17:28 Brought beds, basins, clay pots, wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans, lentils, and roasted seeds.
2 Samuel 17:29 Honey, butter, sheep, and cow cheese for David and his people to eat because they were hungry, tired, and thirsty in the desert.

2 Samuel 18:1 David counted the people with him and put leaders in charge of groups of a thousand and groups of a hundred.
2 Samuel 18:2 David sent a third of the troops with Joab, another third with Abishai, Joab's brother, and the last third with Ittai the Gittite. The king told the people, "I will definitely come with you too."
2 Samuel 18:3 The people said, "You must not go out: if we run away, they won't bother with us; even if half of us die, they won't bother. But you are as valuable as ten thousand of us. So it's better for you to help us from inside the city."
2 Samuel 18:4 The king said to them, "I will do what you think is best." The king stood by the gate, and all the people came out in groups of hundreds and thousands.
2 Samuel 18:5 The king told Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, "Please be kind to the young man Absalom for me." Everyone heard when the king ordered the captains to take care of Absalom.
2 Samuel 18:6 The people went out to fight against Israel, and the battle happened in the forest of Ephraim.
2 Samuel 18:7 The Israelites were killed by David's men, and that day 20,000 men died in a big battle.
2 Samuel 18:8 The fight spread out across the land, and the forest took more lives that day than the sword.
2 Samuel 18:9 Absalom met David's servants. Absalom rode on a mule, which passed under a big oak tree's dense branches, and his head got stuck in the oak. He was left hanging between the sky and the ground, and the mule under him ran off.
2 Samuel 18:10 A man saw this, told Joab, and said, "Look, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak tree."
2 Samuel 18:11 Joab said to the man who told him, "You saw him, so why didn't you kill him right there? I would have given you ten silver coins and a belt."
2 Samuel 18:12 The man said to Joab, "Even if I got a thousand silver coins, I wouldn't hurt the king's son because we heard the king tell you, Abishai, and Ittai, 'Don't harm the young man Absalom.'"
2 Samuel 18:13 Otherwise, I would have lied about my own life, because nothing is hidden from the king, and you would have opposed me.
2 Samuel 18:14 Joab said, "I can't wait like this with you." He grabbed three sharp rods and stuck them into Absalom's heart, while Absalom was still alive in the oak tree.
2 Samuel 18:15 Ten young men carrying Joab's weapons surrounded Absalom, attacked him, and killed him.
2 Samuel 18:16 Joab sounded the trumpet, and the people stopped chasing Israel because Joab held them back.
2 Samuel 18:17 They took Absalom, threw him into a big hole in the forest, and put a huge pile of stones on him; then all Israel ran away to their own tents.
2 Samuel 18:18 While he was alive, Absalom set up a monument for himself in the King's Valley because he said, "I have no son to carry on my name." He named the monument after himself, and it is still called Absalom's Monument to this day.
2 Samuel 18:19 Then Ahimaaz, Zadok's son, said, "Let me run now and tell the king that God has taken revenge against his enemies for him."
2 Samuel 18:20 Joab told him, "You won't bring news today, but you will bring news another day. Today you won't bring any news, because the king's son has died."
2 Samuel 18:21 Joab said to Cushi, "Go tell the king what you have seen." Cushi bowed to Joab and ran.
2 Samuel 18:22 Ahimaaz, son of Zadok, said to Joab again, "Please, let me run after Cushi." Joab asked, "Why do you want to run, my son, when you have no news?"
2 Samuel 18:23 He said, "Please let me run." And the person told him, "Run." So Ahimaaz ran through the flat land and passed Cushi.
2 Samuel 18:24 David sat between the two gates, and the lookout went up to the roof over the gate, onto the wall, looked up, and saw a man running by himself.
2 Samuel 18:25 The guard called out and informed the king. The king said, "If he is alone, he brings news." He hurried and got closer.
2 Samuel 18:26 The guard saw another man running and called to the gatekeeper, "Look, another man is running by himself." The king said, "He too is bringing news."
2 Samuel 18:27 The lookout said, I think the way the first one runs looks like Ahimaaz, Zadok's son. And the king said, He's a good man, coming with good news.
2 Samuel 18:28 Ahimaaz called out and said to the king, "Everything is fine." He bowed to the ground before the king and said, "Praise be to God, your God, who has handed over the men who raised their hand against my king."
2 Samuel 18:29 The king asked, "Is Absalom, the young man, okay?" Ahimaaz replied, "When Joab sent the king's servant and me, your servant, I saw a big commotion, but I didn't know what it was about."
2 Samuel 18:30 The king told him, "Move over there and wait." So he moved aside and waited.
2 Samuel 18:31 Look, Cushi came and Cushi said, "News, my king: for God has punished those who were against you today."
2 Samuel 18:32 The king asked Cushi, "Is the young man Absalom okay?" Cushi replied, "May all the king's enemies and those who wish to harm you be like that young man."
2 Samuel 18:33 The king was deeply upset and walked up to the room above the gate, crying. As he walked, he said, "Oh my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom, I wish I had died instead of you, oh Absalom, my son, my son!"

2 Samuel 19:1 Someone told Joab, "Look, the king is crying and grieving for Absalom."
2 Samuel 19:2 That day, the people's victory changed to sadness because they heard that the king was greatly saddened about his son.
2 Samuel 19:3 That day, the people sneaked into the city like those who, feeling ashamed, quietly escape during a fight.
2 Samuel 19:4 The king covered his face and cried out loudly, "My son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom!"
2 Samuel 19:5 Joab went to the king's house and said, "Today you have embarrassed all your servants who have saved your life, your sons' and daughters' lives, your wives' lives, and your concubines' lives."
2 Samuel 19:6 Because you love your enemies and hate your friends, you have shown today that you care for neither leaders nor followers. Today I realize that if Absalom had survived and all of us had died, you would have been happy.
2 Samuel 19:7 Get up now, go out, and talk kindly to your servants, because I promise by God, if you don't go out, no one will stay with you tonight, and this will be worse for you than all the bad things that have happened to you since you were young until now.
2 Samuel 19:8 The king got up and sat at the gate. People told everyone, "Look, the king is sitting at the gate." All the people went to see the king, because the Israelites had all run away to their tents.
2 Samuel 19:9 All the people across Israel's tribes were arguing, saying, "The king rescued us from our enemies and saved us from the Philistines; but now he has run away from the land because of Absalom."
2 Samuel 19:10 Absalom, who we made our leader, has died in battle. So why don't you talk about bringing the king back?
2 Samuel 19:11 King David sent a message to Zadok and Abiathar, the priests, telling them, "Talk to the leaders of Judah and ask them, 'Why are you the last ones to bring the king back to his home when all of Israel is talking about it, even at his home?'"
2 Samuel 19:12 You are my brothers, you are my own flesh and bones: so why are you the last to bring back the king?
2 Samuel 19:13 Tell Amasa, aren't you my family, my own flesh and bone? May God deal with me, even worse, if you are not always the army commander instead of Joab.
2 Samuel 19:14 He made all the men of Judah agree as one; they told the king, "Come back, you and all your helpers."
2 Samuel 19:15 The king went back and arrived at the Jordan River. People from Judah went to Gilgal to meet the king and help him cross the Jordan.
2 Samuel 19:16 Shimei, Gera's son from the tribe of Benjamin, who was from Bahurim, hurried and went down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
2 Samuel 19:17 A thousand men from Benjamin were with him, along with Ziba, a servant from Saul's house, and his fifteen sons and twenty servants; they crossed the Jordan River ahead of the king.
2 Samuel 19:18 A ferry boat took the king's family across and did what he wanted. Shimei, Gera's son, bowed before the king when he crossed the Jordan.
2 Samuel 19:19 He said to the king, "Please don't blame me for doing wrong, and don't remember the bad thing I did when you, the king, left Jerusalem. Don't keep it in your mind."
2 Samuel 19:20 I, your servant, know I have sinned. That's why I am the first one from Joseph's family to meet the king today.
2 Samuel 19:21 But Abishai, Zeruiah's son, replied, "Shouldn't Shimei die for cursing God's chosen one?"
2 Samuel 19:22 David said, "What's my business with you, sons of Zeruiah? Why are you causing trouble for me today? Should anyone be killed in Israel today? Don't I know that today I am king over Israel?"
2 Samuel 19:23 So the king told Shimei, "You will not die." And the king promised him that.
2 Samuel 19:24 Mephibosheth, Saul's son, met the king without caring for his feet, cutting his beard, or washing his clothes since the king left until he returned safely.
2 Samuel 19:25 When he arrived in Jerusalem to see the king, the king asked him, "Why didn't you come with me, Mephibosheth?"
2 Samuel 19:26 He replied, "My king, my servant tricked me. I planned to saddle a donkey to ride and go to the king, because I am lame."
2 Samuel 19:27 He has lied about me to you, the king, but you, the king, are like an angel of God. So do what you think is right.
2 Samuel 19:28 Everyone in my father's family was as good as dead before you, the king, but you allowed me, your servant, to eat at your table. So, what right do I have to ask anything more from you, the king?
2 Samuel 19:29 The king said to him, "Why do you talk more about your issues? I've decided, you and Ziba will share the land."
2 Samuel 19:30 Mephibosheth told the king, "Yes, let him take everything, since you, the king, have returned home safely."
2 Samuel 19:31 Barzillai from Gilead left Rogelim and crossed the Jordan River with the king to help him get across.
2 Samuel 19:32 Barzillai was a very old man, eighty years old, and he had given the king food while he stayed at Mahanaim, because he was a very important man.
2 Samuel 19:33 The king told Barzillai, "Come with me and I will take care of you in Jerusalem."
2 Samuel 19:34 Barzillai asked the king, "How long do I have left to live that I should go with the king to Jerusalem?"
2 Samuel 19:35 I am eighty years old today: and can I tell right from wrong? Can your servant taste what I eat or drink? Can I still hear the voices of singers, both men and women? Why then should I be a burden to you, the king?
2 Samuel 19:36 I will cross the Jordan River with the king for a short distance. Why should the king give me such a reward?
2 Samuel 19:37 Please let me, your servant, go back to die in my city near my parents' graves. But let Chimham go with you, and you can do for him what you think is best.
2 Samuel 19:38 The king said, "Chimham will come with me, and I will be good to him as you wish. Whatever you ask of me, I will do for you."
2 Samuel 19:39 All the people crossed the Jordan River. When the king crossed, he kissed Barzillai and blessed him, then Barzillai went back to his home.
2 Samuel 19:40 Then the king continued to Gilgal, with Chimham going with him; all the people of Judah led the king, and also half the people of Israel.
2 Samuel 19:41 Look, all the men of Israel came to the king and asked him, "Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, secretly take you, the king, his family, and all of David's men across the Jordan river?"
2 Samuel 19:42 All the men of Judah replied to the men of Israel, "The king is related to us, so why are you angry about this? Did we eat at the king's expense, or did he give us any present?"
2 Samuel 19:43 The men of Israel responded to the men of Judah, saying, "We have ten shares in the king and a stronger claim on David than you. So why did you look down on us? Why wasn't our advice considered first in bringing back our king?" But the men of Judah's responses were harsher than those of the men of Israel.

2 Samuel 20:1 A bad man named Sheba, Bichri's son from the tribe of Benjamin, was there. He blew a trumpet and shouted, "We don't belong with David or share in Jesse's son's inheritance. Everyone go home, Israel!"
2 Samuel 20:2 Every man of Israel left David and followed Sheba, Bichri's son. But the men of Judah stayed loyal to their king, from the Jordan River to Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 20:3 David returned to his home in Jerusalem; he brought the ten women - his concubines he left to look after the house - and placed them under guard, providing food for them, but he did not sleep with them. They lived in confinement until they died as widows.
2 Samuel 20:4 The king told Amasa, "Gather the men of Judah in three days and make sure you are here."
2 Samuel 20:5 So Amasa went to gather the men of Judah, but he took longer than the time he was given.
2 Samuel 20:6 David told Abishai, "Sheba, Bichri's son, will cause us more trouble than Absalom did. Take your master's men and go after him, or he'll find strong cities to hide in and slip away from us."
2 Samuel 20:7 Joab's soldiers, the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the strong warriors left Jerusalem to chase Sheba, Bichri's son.
2 Samuel 20:8 When they were at the big rock in Gibeon, Amasa walked ahead. Joab wore his coat with a belt tied around it, and a sword in its sheath on his hips; as he moved, it dropped out.
2 Samuel 20:9 Joab asked Amasa, "Are you well, my brother?" Then Joab grabbed Amasa's beard with his right hand to kiss him.
2 Samuel 20:10 Amasa did not notice the sword in Joab's hand; Joab stabbed him in the side, his insides spilled out, and he did not stab him again; Amasa died. Joab and his brother Abishai chased after Sheba, Bichri's son.
2 Samuel 20:11 One of Joab's soldiers stood there and said, "Anyone who supports Joab or is on David's side should follow Joab."
2 Samuel 20:12 Amasa was rolling in blood in the middle of the road. When the man noticed that everyone stopped, he took Amasa off the road into the field and covered him with a cloth because he saw that everyone passing by stopped.
2 Samuel 20:13 After he was moved from the road, all the people followed Joab to chase after Sheba, Bichri's son.
2 Samuel 20:14 He traveled through all Israel's tribes to Abel, Bethmaachah, and the Berite lands. They joined together and followed him.
2 Samuel 20:15 They surrounded him at Abel Bethmaachah, built a ramp against the city which reached the outer wall, and all Joab's troops attacked the wall to knock it down.
2 Samuel 20:16 A smart woman from the city shouted, "Listen, please ask Joab to come here so I can talk to him."
2 Samuel 20:17 When he got close to her, the woman asked, "Are you Joab?" He replied, "Yes, I am." Then she said to him, "Listen to what I have to say." He answered, "I am listening."
2 Samuel 20:18 Then she said, "People used to say long ago, 'They will definitely seek advice at Abel,' and that's how they settled the issue."
2 Samuel 20:19 I am one of those who are peaceful and loyal in Israel; you want to destroy a city and a mother in Israel: why do you want to consume God's heritage?
2 Samuel 20:20 Joab replied, "No, no way; I don't want to ruin or destroy anything."
2 Samuel 20:21 This isn't true: a man from the hill country of Ephraim, named Sheba son of Bichri, has turned against the king, against David. Give us just him, and I will leave the city. The woman told Joab, Look, his head will be thrown to you over the wall.
2 Samuel 20:22 The woman shared her wise plan with everyone. They beheaded Sheba, son of Bichri, and threw his head to Joab. Joab sounded the trumpet, and everyone left the city to go to their own tents. Then Joab went back to see the king in Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 20:23 Joab led all of Israel's army; Benaiah, Jehoiada's son, led the Cherethites and Pelethites.
2 Samuel 20:24 Adoram was in charge of forced labor, and Jehoshaphat, Ahilud's son, was the historian.
2 Samuel 20:25 Sheva was the secretary; Zadok and Abiathar were the priests.
2 Samuel 20:26 Ira the Jairite was also a leading official in David's service.

2 Samuel 21:1 There was a food shortage during David's time for three years in a row, and David asked God. God said, "It is because of Saul and his violent family, for he killed the Gibeonites."
2 Samuel 21:2 The king summoned the Gibeonites and spoke to them. The Gibeonites were not part of the Israelites but were leftover Amorites. The Israelites had made a promise to them, but Saul wanted to kill them to show his commitment to the Israelites and Judah.
2 Samuel 21:3 David said to the Gibeonites, "What can I do for you? And how can I make things right so you will bless God's people?"
2 Samuel 21:4 The Gibeonites told him, "We don't want any silver or gold from Saul or his family, and you shouldn't kill anyone in Israel for us." He replied, "Tell me what you want, and I'll do it for you."
2 Samuel 21:5 The people told the king, "The man who destroyed us and planned for us to be wiped out from all over Israel,"
2 Samuel 21:6 Give us seven of his sons, and we will hang them before God in Saul's town of Gibeah, whom God chose. And the king said, I will give them.
2 Samuel 21:7 The king did not harm Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son and Saul's grandson, because of the promise that David and Jonathan had made before God.
2 Samuel 21:8 The king took Rizpah's two sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth, and the five sons Michal raised for Adriel.
2 Samuel 21:9 God let the Gibeonites capture them, and they hung them on a hill before God. All seven died at the same time during the early days of the barley harvest.
2 Samuel 21:10 Rizpah, Aiah's daughter, laid a rough cloth on a rock. She kept it there from harvest start until rain fell from the sky. She did not let birds land on it during the day or wild animals at night.
2 Samuel 21:11 David was told about what Rizpah, Aiah's daughter and Saul's concubine, had done.
2 Samuel 21:12 David retrieved the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from the people of Jabeshgilead, who had taken them from Bethshan where the Philistines hung them after killing Saul in Gilboa.
2 Samuel 21:13 He brought up the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from there; they also gathered the bones of those who were hanged.
2 Samuel 21:14 They buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in the land of Benjamin at Zelah, in the tomb of Saul's father Kish. They did everything the king ordered. After that, God answered prayers for the land.
2 Samuel 21:15 The Philistines went to war with Israel again; David and his men fought against them, and David became very tired.
2 Samuel 21:16 Ishbibenob, one of the giant's sons, had a spear that weighed three hundred shekels of brass. He wore a new sword and planned to kill David.
2 Samuel 21:17 Abishai, son of Zeruiah, helped him and struck the Philistine, killing him. Then David's men promised him, "You will not go with us to fight anymore, so you do not put out Israel's light."
2 Samuel 21:18 After this, another battle happened with the Philistines at Gob. Then Sibbechai the Hushathite killed Saph, who was one of the giant's sons.
2 Samuel 21:19 Another battle happened in Gob with the Philistines. There, Elhanan, son of Jaareoregim from Bethlehem, killed Goliath the Gittite's brother, who had a spear with a shaft like a weaver's tool.
2 Samuel 21:20 Another battle took place in Gath. There was a very tall man there who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot—24 in total. He was also a descendant of the giant.
2 Samuel 21:21 When he challenged Israel, Jonathan, David's nephew and Shimeah's son, killed him.
2 Samuel 21:22 These four were born to the giant in Gath, and were killed by David and his men.

2 Samuel 22:1 David sang to God this song when God saved him from all his enemies and from Saul.
2 Samuel 22:2 He said, "God is my rock, my fortress, and my savior."
2 Samuel 22:3 God is my protector; I will trust in him: he is my shield, my strength to save me, my safe place, and my shelter, my savior; you protect me from harm.
2 Samuel 22:4 I will call on God, who deserves praise: so I will be saved from my enemies.
2 Samuel 22:5 When the waves of death surrounded me, the attacks of evil men scared me.
2 Samuel 22:6 The pains of death surrounded me; death's traps were stopping me.
2 Samuel 22:7 In my trouble, I called to God and shouted for help. He heard my voice from his place, and my call reached his ears.
2 Samuel 22:8 The earth shook and quaked; the bases of the sky trembled and moved because God was angry.
2 Samuel 22:9 Smoke rose from his nose, and fire from his mouth consumed; coals blazed from it.
2 Samuel 22:10 He bent the skies and came down; darkness was under his feet.
2 Samuel 22:11 He rode on a cherub and flew; he appeared on the wings of the wind.
2 Samuel 22:12 He made dark shelters around him, with dark waters and heavy clouds in the sky.
2 Samuel 22:13 Bright light from God made coals of fire start burning.
2 Samuel 22:14 God thundered from heaven, and the highest one spoke aloud.
2 Samuel 22:15 He shot arrows and spread them out; he sent lightning and confused them.
2 Samuel 22:16 The paths of the sea were shown, the base of the earth was uncovered, when God scolded, with the strong wind from his nose.
2 Samuel 22:17 He reached down from on high and took hold of me; he pulled me out of deep waters.
2 Samuel 22:18 God saved me from my powerful enemy and from those who hated me because they were too strong for me.
2 Samuel 22:19 They stopped me when I was in trouble, but God supported me.
2 Samuel 22:20 God brought me out into a spacious place; he freed me because he was pleased with me.
2 Samuel 22:21 God rewarded me for doing right; he repaid me because my hands were clean.
2 Samuel 22:22 I have followed God's paths and have not turned away from my God to do wrong.
2 Samuel 22:23 I kept all God's rules in mind, and I did not turn away from his laws.
2 Samuel 22:24 I was also honest before God, and I have kept myself from doing wrong.
2 Samuel 22:25 So God has rewarded me for doing right; He has seen my clean actions.
2 Samuel 22:26 You are kind to those who are kind, and you are good to those who are good.
2 Samuel 22:27 You are pure to those who are pure, but you seem not good to those who are not good.
2 Samuel 22:28 You will save those who are suffering, but you are watching the proud, to bring them down.
2 Samuel 22:29 You are my light, God, and God will brighten my darkness.
2 Samuel 22:30 With your help, I have charged through an army; with my God, I have jumped over a wall.
2 Samuel 22:31 God's way is perfect; his word is proven; he protects all who trust in him.
2 Samuel 22:32 Who is God besides the LORD? Who is strong like our God?
2 Samuel 22:33 God is my strength and power, and he makes my path perfect.
2 Samuel 22:34 He makes my feet as sure as a deer's: and places me on high ground.
2 Samuel 22:35 He teaches my hands to fight; so that my arms can break a steel bow.
2 Samuel 22:36 You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your kindness has made me strong.
2 Samuel 22:37 You have made my steps wide beneath me; so my feet did not slide.
2 Samuel 22:38 I chased my enemies and defeated them; I did not stop until I had completely beaten them.
2 Samuel 22:39 I have destroyed them and injured them so they could not get up; yes, they have fallen beneath my feet.
2 Samuel 22:40 You have given me strength to fight; you have made those who attacked me fall under my control.
2 Samuel 22:41 You have also let me defeat my enemies and destroy those who hate me.
2 Samuel 22:42 They looked for help, but no one could save them; they even cried to God, but he did not respond.
2 Samuel 22:43 I crushed them into dust on the ground, stomped them into mud on the street, and scattered them everywhere.
2 Samuel 22:44 You have also saved me from my people's conflicts and kept me as the leader of nations; people I didn't know will serve me.
2 Samuel 22:45 Foreigners will come to me and obey as soon as they hear me.
2 Samuel 22:46 Foreigners will grow weak and be scared from their hiding spots.
2 Samuel 22:47 God lives; praise to my rock; and may the God who saves me be lifted high.
2 Samuel 22:48 God avenges me and makes other people submit to me.
2 Samuel 22:49 You lead me away from my enemies; you lift me up above my opponents; you save me from violent people.
2 Samuel 22:50 So I will thank you, God, among the nations, and sing praises to your name.
2 Samuel 22:51 He is the saving tower for his king and shows kindness to his chosen one, David, and his descendants forever.

2 Samuel 23:1 These are the final words of David. David, Jesse's son, spoke, the man lifted up, chosen by the God of Jacob, and Israel's beloved song writer, said.
2 Samuel 23:2 God's Spirit spoke through me, and His words were on my tongue.
2 Samuel 23:3 The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me: Whoever leads people must be fair, leading with respect for God.
2 Samuel 23:4 He will be like the light of dawn when the sun rises, on a cloudless morning; like fresh grass growing from the ground when the sun shines brightly after rain.
2 Samuel 23:5 Even though my family is not close to God, He has made a lasting agreement with me, well-planned and certain; this is all that saves me and all I want, even though He doesn't make it prosper.
2 Samuel 23:6 The wicked will all be like thorns pushed aside, because they cannot be picked up with hands.
2 Samuel 23:7 Anyone who touches them must be armed with iron and a spear's shaft; they will be completely burned with fire right there.
2 Samuel 23:8 These are the names of David's strong warriors: The leader is the Tachmonite, who sat in the main chair, was Adino the Eznite. He raised his spear and beat eight hundred enemies at once.
2 Samuel 23:9 After him came Eleazar, son of Dodo the Ahohite. He was one of David's three brave warriors. He stood up to the Philistines gathered for battle when the Israelites had retreated.
2 Samuel 23:10 He got up, fought the Philistines until his hand got tired, and his hand stuck to the sword. God gave a great victory that day, and the people followed him just to take things from the defeated.
2 Samuel 23:11 After him came Shammah, Agee the Hararite's son. The Philistines grouped into a force at a field of lentils, but the people ran away from the Philistines.
2 Samuel 23:12 He stood in the middle of the field, defended it, killed the Philistines, and God gave a great victory.
2 Samuel 23:13 Three of the top thirty soldiers went to see David at Adullam cave during harvest time, while the Philistine army camped in Rephaim Valley.
2 Samuel 23:14 David was in a stronghold, and the Philistines' fort was in Bethlehem at that time.
2 Samuel 23:15 David wished and said, "I want someone to bring me water from the Bethlehem well near the gate!"
2 Samuel 23:16 The three strong men fought through the Philistine army, and got water from the Bethlehem well near the gate, and brought it to David. But he wouldn't drink it and instead poured it out to God.
